articles.title: The Developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP): Continuous Word Reading Difficulty Estimates of the 9,961 Most Frequently Printed English Words for US Children
articles.authors: Donald Compton; Jay Rueckl; Laura Steacy; Noam Siegelman; Ashley Edwards; Yaacov Petscher; Nicole Patton Terry; Matthew James Cooper Borkenhagen; Chelsea Starke
articles.abstract: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) is a database comprising word reading data for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for children, including continuous IRT-based estimates of word reading difficulty, accompanying word characteristics, and raw trial-level data. Data on isolated word reading accuracy were collected from 1,907 children in grades 1-5 across multiple US sites. Each child read a list of words ranging from 250 to 500 items depending on reading skill (less proficient children were often unable to finish the entire list of words), with each list representing the full distribution of word difficulties oversampled for words at the child’s reading level. Each child also attempted 99 linking items representing the full distribution of word difficulties. A total of 631,322 total responses were collected with the average child providing 336. For the final sample of words, the average number of responses per word for the 9,862 non-linking items was 47.14 (range of 10-592) and for the 99 linking items the average was 1681.42 (range of 1083-1907). A Rasch model, with planned missing design, was fit to children’s responses on the word list and linking item responses. This introduction describes the motivation for this project; the methods used for data collecting; the analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty across words; descriptive statistics of the relational database and initial behavioral results; and a publicly available search engine providing searchable access to the word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics.

articles.title: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI: A Theoretical Framework for Memory, Metacognition, and Consumer Decision-Making
articles.authors: Chen Chen; Kristy Hamilton; Jacob T. Fisher
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow. A seven-stage delegation continuum maps increasing levels of offloading, and a value-based cost-benefit framework identifies its antecedents and the moderators that shape how consumers weigh them. We propose three clusters of outcomes. First, offloading weakens memory for brands and product attributes while strengthening memory for AI-generated summaries. Second, it inflates metacognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, producing AI-induced overconfidence that reduces further information-seeking. Third, effects on decision quality depend on AI reliability: when AI is unreliable, verifying AI recommendations imposes cognitive and emotional costs but can restore impaired memory and recalibrate inflated confidence. Seven propositions and three long-term conjectures extend these effects to consumer autonomy, competence erosion, and brand loyalty. Together, the CogOffload framework positions advertising in the era of Gen-AI as operating within a distributed system of human and artificial cognition.

articles.title: Being Observed by a Tutor Enhances Foreign Speech Production Learning in Video-Mediated Training
articles.authors: Qin Li; Piia Astikainen; Xueqiao Li; Shun Liu
articles.abstract: Social presence, particularly awareness of being observed by a tutor, may enhance learners’ engagement and attention during foreign language practice, but its effects on learning and associated neural activity remain poorly understood. We investigated whether learners’ (n = 32) awareness of being observed by a tutor influences foreign speech learning in a short (11-min) video-mediated listen-and-repeat training for Mandarin words. In the online group, learners knew the tutor could see them, whereas in the offline group, they knew the tutor could neither see nor hear them. Tone production was assessed before, during, and after training, and tone identification before and after training. Electroencephalography and autonomic activity were recorded during training. Tone production accuracy improved from pre- to post-training in the online group only, whereas tone identification improved similarly in both groups. Posterior alpha power increased during training in the offline group but did not change significantly in the online group. Together, these findings suggest that awareness of being observed by a tutor may support foreign language speech production learning in video-mediated settings. The accompanying differences in posterior alpha activity further indicate that the social context of learning is associated with differences in neural activity during practice.

articles.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review
articles.authors: Olivia Andrews; Mathilde E. Brons; I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; H.M. Koning Ina; Sophie Mary; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract:
Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media. This
scientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youth
and used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.
Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns and
collaboration networks. Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately
(58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension. Only
2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions. Interventions predominantly focused on content and
conduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions,
privacy, digital rights, and commercialization. Collaboration patterns were fragmented, with
researchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on a
shared conceptual foundation. These findings suggest that current interventions cover only part
of the 4C framework. Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensional
interventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.

articles.title: From Individual Gains to Collective Losses? The Socially Corrosive Path of Generative AI
articles.authors: Markus Langer; Igor Grossmann
articles.abstract: AI tools including generative AI (genAI) and agentic AI promise individual productivity gains, and users experience them as a resource that makes them more capable. However, research documents a robust social evaluation penalty for individual genAI use: people who use genAI, or are suspected of doing so, are judged as less competent, less diligent, and less caring. We argue that these judgments, followed through to their behavioral consequences, outline a socially corrosive path of collective genAI use. Along this path, when people substitute human contact with genAI and devalue what colleagues produce, relational interdependence, metaknowledge, and resulting opportunities for scalable collective intelligence decline, whereas trust erodes through a cycle of concealment, suspicion, policing, and blame. Current technology design and productivity narratives amplify these dynamics. We caution against waiting for genAI use to normalize and propose countermeasures: designing genAI for collective functioning, resisting the productivity trap, and making the social norms of genAI use explicit.

articles.title: Can LLMs Grow Like Children? A Developmental Analysis of Capability Trajectories in Language Model Training
articles.authors: Ran An; Tingting Chung; Klaus Libertus
articles.abstract: Within two years, an infant who can barely lift her head learns to sit, reach, and walk. Developmental science found that this growth is both continuous and phased: skills improve smoothly, yet the pace of improvement changes at identifiable ages, and the field built statistical tools to locate those changes. Language models also transform across training, and whether their capabilities grow smoothly or in jumps is actively debated. The present study argues that the developmental answer applies to artificial learners as well, and that the developmental tools can show it. We apply an analysis pipeline built for infant motor development to the training trajectories of 16 open-source language models, each tested at 27 points during training on five benchmarks. The results mirror the infant findings. Growth is continuous but organized into phases, and transitions cluster at a small set of shared points that are deployed differently across domains. Growth proceeds slowly, then rapidly, then slowly, and models differ reliably in developmental rate. Unlike infants, those rate differences are almost entirely explained by model size. The transitions also survive changes of measurement scale, and on a continuous measure they appear earlier and more sharply than on accuracy. The paper contributes a formal test for phase structure in capability growth, a construct mapping between infant development and language model development, and evidence that phase structure may be a shared property of learning systems.

articles.title: Effect of Disclaimers on the Public Perception of AI-Generated Medical Advice: Two Preregistered Survey Experiments
articles.authors: Moritz Reis; Florian Reis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used by the public as a source of medical advice, yet they can produce plausible but incorrect output. Disclaimers about the limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) are the most common safeguard and are also anchored in regulatory frameworks such as the European Union's AI Act. Whether disclaimers change how laypeople perceive and act on AI-generated medical advice, however, is unknown. We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396). Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer. Study 1 used the standard disclaimer of a popular chatbot; study 2 used a stronger disclaimer that explicitly highlighted the higher risk of error compared with physicians and required participants to confirm having read it. Participants rated the advice’s empathy, reliability, and comprehensibility and their willingness to follow it. In study 1, the disclaimer did not significantly affect any outcome (all p > .17). In study 2, it did not significantly affect empathy, reliability, or comprehensibility (all p > .19). Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower with the disclaimer (p = .039), but this effect did not remain significant after correcting for multiple testing. Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the two disclaimers. Disclaimers may thus serve mainly as transparency and liability measures and should not be relied on alone to protect users. Alternatives, such as communicating uncertainty within the response and strengthening AI literacy, deserve evaluation.

articles.title: How to Design a Panel Study for Investigating Bivariate Dynamics Using Continuous-Time Modeling
articles.authors: Nuria Real-Brioso; Eduardo Estrada
articles.abstract: Designing effective longitudinal panel studies to capture bivariate dynamics requires making informed decisions about how many measurements to collect and when to collect them. This study examines how design choices, concretely sample size, number of repeated measures, and various aspects of the temporal sampling schedule, influence the recovery of bivariate dynamic parameters in panel data analyzed using a Continuous-Time Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CT-RI-CLPM). Through a Monte Carlo simulation, we tested a range of generating population parameters. We proposed a novel approach for planning sampling schedules: the Short-and-Long Lags design (SHALL) which deliberately mixes closely spaced and widely spaced intervals that continuous time models can accommodate. SHALL schedules are simple to understand and implement, and consistently ranked among the best sampling schedules in many scenarios. Our findings suggest that the number of repeated measurements and sample size significantly impact parameter recovery, particularly for cross-lagged effects, which exhibited low estimation efficiency even in the most favorable conditions, leading to low statistical power. We provide actionable recommendations for researchers planning panel data studies, along with open-source R code to facilitate the design of SHALL sampling schedules. We also provide R code to implement a CT-RI-CLPM to new data sets. An empirical example illustrates the application of such a model to data from an empirical panel study relating self-esteem and depression. This work contributes evidence-based guidance for improving the design and analysis of longitudinal panel studies using continuous-time modeling.

articles.title: Invariant agreement attraction effects: Distance and RC modification manipulations in Czech
articles.authors: Radim Lacina; Jakub Dotlacil
articles.abstract: Agreement attraction in comprehension often manifests itself as a speed-up in the of processing ungrammatical sentences where a verb carries the wrong number feature when a noun of the verb-matching number —the attractor—intervenes. The effect has been claimed to be insensitive to increased linear distance between the attractor and the agreement target. Recent studies on Czech found weak attraction effects attested only with case syncretic attractors. In two self-paced reading experiments with Czech comprehenders, we tested whether including material between the attractor and the verb could modulate attraction depending on whether the material was reinforcing the attractor's features or not. In Experiment 1, we aimed to increase attraction strength by modifying the attractor with a relative clause, giving it the subject feature and reinforcing its plurality. In Experiment 2, we matched the increased distance employed in Experiment 1 with feature-inert material to see if attraction was maintained. Our Bayes factor analysis provided us with evidence of a small attraction effect in the both experiments that did not differ meaningfully between the two. We therefore show that Czech exhibits online number attraction but of a tiny effect size. Our results further replicate earlier findings that distance does not affect agreement attraction in comprehension, as our effect sizes were comparable between the two experiments as well with previous work on Czech. Finally, they show that modifying attractors with relative clauses does not increase the strength of attraction speed-ups.

articles.title: A Three-Wave RI-CLPM Linking Adolescent Affect and their Engagement with Sustainable Development
articles.authors: Richard Anthony Inman; Sara Ribeiro de Faria; Paulo Moreira
articles.abstract: This study examines reciprocal relationships between affect and engagement and disengagement with sustainable development in a cohort of 580 Portuguese adolescents assessed serendipitously before COVID-19 (ages 12-13), during lockdown (ages 13-14), and approximately one year after lockdown (ages 13-14). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling (RI-CLPM) distinguished stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. Adolescents with higher negative affect generally reported lower engagement and higher disengagement. Within individuals, higher-than-usual negative affect before the pandemic predicted greater subsequent disengagement during lockdown. In turn, higher-than-usual negative affect during lockdown predicted greater subsequent engagement. No cross-lagged effects involving positive affect or from engagement or disengagement to affect were statistically significant. The findings suggest that negative affect may precede different responses to sustainable development across contextual conditions. Efforts to promote engagement should therefore consider adolescents’ emotional experiences alongside their circumstances, rather than assume that negative affect necessarily undermines engagement or that evoking it will encourage sustainable action.

articles.title: On Bias in Detecting Bias: A Signal Detection Analysis of Attributions to Gender Discrimination
articles.authors: Marie Jakob; Anat Shechter; Jimmy Calanchini; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles.abstract:
Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of Signal Detection Theory (SDT), with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers’ ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers’ judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical SDT analyses of attributions to
discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1 to 3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2 to 4) inform observers’ response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1 to 3), which reflects observers’ determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing.

articles.title: Development Insights and User Experience of a Preventive Digital Parenting Intervention for Adolescent Mental Health
articles.authors: Rick van Logchem; Crystal R. Smit; Anne Bülow; Hanneke Scholten; Bart Soenens; Loes Keijsers
articles.abstract:
Background: Despite being hailed as a promising avenue for preventing increasingly prevalent adolescent mental health problems, digital parenting interventions to strengthen adolescent mental well-being remain scarce. How such interventions are developed and experienced by end-users provides key insights for their later implementation and contextualizes information on their effectiveness, yet little systemic evidence is available.
Objective: To inform optimal development and aid careful evaluation of digital parenting interventions, this preregistered multimethod study served three aims. First, to identify theoretical, functional, and user-derived lessons for digital parenting interventions for adolescent mental well-being, distilled from the challenges of developing a novel digital parenting intervention. Second, to examine user experience in terms of feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness as early markers of implementation success. Third, to understand whether user experience is linked to characteristics of the intervention (i.e., universal versus personalized delivery), parents (e.g., openness to advice), or adolescents (e.g., depressive symptoms).
Methods: Development of the intervention was based on Self-Determination Theory and followed an iterative process, including focus groups with parents and adolescents, a pilot study among n = 12 families and subsequent exit-interviews, and a brainstorm session with experts (n = 6). The intervention was evaluated among parents (N = 199, Mage = 47.6, SDage = 4.7), resulting in administrative and daily diary data of user experience (feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness). Baseline data were used to test whether intervention, parent, and adolescent characteristics related to user experience.
Results: Findings suggest that adolescent perspectives align with the tenets of self-determination theory as a framework that can be translated to concrete advice for parents, that the frequency and delivery of advice should fit family routines, and parental agency and choice were important user needs. Feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness were sufficient according to our preregistered criteria, but there was substantial heterogeneity between parents and within parents (across days). User experience did not differ between a personalized and universal version of the intervention. Parents who were generally more open to advice, and parents of boys, younger adolescents, and less depressed adolescents evaluated the intervention more favorably. 
Conclusions: Findings suggest that the fit between our intervention and parents differed substantially across parents, and from tip tot tip, highlighting the need for further refinement of our digital parenting interventions before implementation, and the consideration of user experience throughout development.

articles.title: Designing Around the Human Creative Core: A Construct for Preserving Creative Agency in Human-AI Systems
articles.authors: Eran Barak-Medina
articles.abstract: Generative AI can increasingly perform the parts of professional work where a person's judgment and sense of identity are most engaged. The common design instinct is to automate wherever AI can plausibly take over, treating capability as the test. This efficiency-first instinct can erode the skill, judgment, ownership, and professional identity. Human-Centered AI frameworks show how to structure collaboration and keep people in control, but not which elements of a given workflow sustain a person's creative agency. This paper introduces the Human Creative Core: the subset of workflow elements where a person's cognitive contribution and psychological investment converge, identified through four dimensions, strategic intention, signature judgment, identity and ownership, and developmental function. The construct yields a design principle, complement the core and automate the periphery, and a method for locating the core in a given workflow. The method was taught and applied in a graduate instructional design course, and is demonstrated here across five professional cases. The contribution is a design construct and a repeatable method for building AI that preserves, and can strengthen, a person's creative agency rather than dissolving it.

articles.title: Psychology’s Missing Matter
articles.authors: Oulmann Zerhouni
articles.abstract: Psychology's replication and generalizability shortcomings suggest that, although valuable, statistical and incentive reforms have not stabilized core constructs. I argue that residual implicit dualism, characterized by the acceptance of loosely defined constructs supported by metaphors and weakly connected to biologically specific mechanisms, contributes to this instability. I propose the Materialist Model of Psychological Science (MMPS): a pluralism-friendly framework based on four axioms (physical realization, multi-level constraint, evolutionary plausibility and mechanistic falsifiability). These axioms are operationalized via an eight-criterion ontological audit with phase-based governance (from prototype to maturity). When applied to three illustrative cases: ego depletion, implicit bias, and fear conditioning. The audit reveals a systematic link between mechanistic density (material anchoring, perturbation-sensitive predictions, and cross-context invariance) and replication robustness. The paper outlines complementary reforms, such as mechanism-focused preregistration, invariance profiling in multilab work, perturbation toolkits and open construct registries, that redirect theory building towards cumulative, vertically integrated knowledge, while safeguarding exploratory diversity through graded evidential expectations. The MMPS adds explicit mechanistic, evolutionary, and perturbational constraints to classical construct validity. The result is a practical foundation that converts diffuse calls for 'better theory' into concrete, auditable criteria for accepting, revising or suspending psychological construct

articles.title: Beyond Participation, Towards Meaningful Inclusion:  An Experience-Sensitive Approach to Inquiry with Children and Young People with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND)
articles.authors: Georgia Pavlopoulou; Elaine McGreevy; Vasileios Sideropoulos
articles.abstract: Contemporary participatory research has focused predominantly on procedural consultation while paying comparatively little attention to how participation is experienced by children and young people (CYP) and research teams, and how those experiences shape knowledge production. We argue that lived experience continues to occupy a peripheral position within scientific knowledge production, often informing rather than constituting evidence. To address this limitation, we propose the Experience-Sensitive Method of Inquiry (ESMI), a methodological orientation that places lived experience at the centre of knowledge production. ESMI is grounded in eight interconnected experience-sensitive dimensions that together provide its epistemological foundation. Central to this framework is participatory reflexivity, conceptualised as an ongoing methodological practice through which researchers examine how relationships, assumptions, environments and methodological choices shape what becomes knowable. Participatory reflexivity therefore functions as the mechanism through which experiential knowledge is recognised, interpreted, and integrated throughout the research process. In practice, ESMI may be operationalised through three interconnected methodological principles: Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC). These principles function as a practical reflexive heuristic for designing, conducting, interpreting and translating participatory research. ESMI shifts attention from whether participation occurs to how participation is experienced and how experiential knowledge influences evidence generation. Although developed in the context of research with CYP with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities, ESMI is intended as a transdisciplinary methodological orientation for experience-informed inquiry. It has two interconnected aims: first, to improve how children and young people with SEND experience research; and second, to strengthen the relevance, interpretability and trustworthiness of the evidence produced. The framework may inform a wide range of methodologies, including trials, longitudinal cohort studies, Delphi studies, experimental research, and qualitative inquiry, from question formulation through to dissemination. The extent to which these proposed benefits are realised remains an empirical question requiring future evaluation.

articles.title: An Individual-Level Paradigm for Research on Deception Cues: An Urgent Proposal
articles.authors: Erik Mac Giolla; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: All psychological theories of deception cues concern explanatory mechanisms at the level of the individual. However, past research on deception cues compares the behavior of people telling the truth and lying at the group level. Unless two conditions are met, that the statistical models do not vary (i) across individuals or (ii) across occasions in time, group-level findings cannot accurately describe the behavior of individuals. We show that these conditions are unlikely to hold for deception cues. This means the current group-level research cannot provide a meaningful test of the individual-level mechanisms key to understanding deception cues. In order to draw meaningful conclusions about these individual-level mechanisms, the field needs a wholly different research paradigm, based on repeated measures designs. We outline a proposal for such an individual-level research agenda and argue that without this development, fundamental questions in deception research will remain unanswered and theories of deception will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Dissociable Effects of Sleep and Memory Suppression on Emotional Memory Processing
articles.authors: Anna Klets; Marcus Harrington; Aidan J Horner; Scott Cairney
articles.abstract: The ability to retrieve memories of adverse events without fully reinstating their associated emotional charge is a hallmark of an adaptive memory system. This decoupling of emotional reactivity from episodic memory has been linked to two key processes: memory suppression during wakefulness and memory consolidation during sleep. Yet, the combined influences of wakeful suppression and sleep-associated memory processing on emotional affect during retrieval are unknown. We sought to address this gap in the current study. Participants learned to associate images of faces with emotionally negative and neutral scenes and then either suppressed or retrieved the scenes when presented with the faces as reminder cues. They then took a nap monitored with polysomnography (nap group) or remained awake for an equivalent period of time in the laboratory (wake group). Before and after the delay, emotional responses to the negative and neutral scenes were evaluated using self-report, skin conductance responses (SCRs) and heart rate deceleration (HRD) to index changes in emotional affect that were attributable to memory suppression and/or sleep-associated consolidation. Memory suppression had no impact on self-reported emotion, SCRs or HRD in either the nap or wake group. However, subjective emotional responses decreased significantly more after sleep than wake. These findings support a role for sleep-associated consolidation in reducing the affective salience of emotional memories.

articles.title: Gambling Marketing in Young Adults’ Digital Media Environments: Exposure, Gambling Risk, and Momentary Responses
articles.authors: Priska Breves; Lauranna Teunissen; Eva van Reijmersdal; Merel Walraven; Martin-Pieter Jansen; Hilde Voorveld
articles.abstract: Advertising restrictions largely remove gambling marketing from mass media, but digital channels, from social media to e-mail, leave room for paid, owned, and earned messages that are difficult to monitor. In a seven-day ecological momentary assessment, 178 Dutch online gamblers aged 18–30 documented encounters with gambling marketing with a screenshot or photo; all 1,377 images were content-analysed. At least one encounter was reported in 42% of assessment intervals and high-risk gamblers recalled more marketing encounters than other participants. Half of the documented marketing came from Instagram or Facebook, half offered a financial inducement, and one in fourteen messages came from unlicensed operators or impersonated licensed brands; high-risk gamblers mostly documented operators’ own posts, the other groups mostly paid ads. At encounters, participants reported a stronger urge to gamble, anticipated more positive outcomes and more escalation of their gambling, and expected to feel less guilty about gambling than in their own unexposed moments. Additionally, gambling was more likely in the same interval as an encounter. Gambling marketing thus remains a routine part of young gamblers’ digital media use and encounters coincide with momentary shifts towards gambling.

articles.title: A Multimodal Study of Screen Use in Adolescents Across Brain Structure, Social Media, and Gaming Use
articles.authors: Wesley Lo; Richard B. Lopez; Benjamin Nephew
articles.abstract: In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

articles.title: Risk in Context: How Weather Influences Consumer Responses to Climate Risk
articles.authors: Zeynep Aslan; Antonia Krefeld-Schwalb; Bram Van den Bergh
articles.abstract:
Protecting homes from increasing climate hazards depends in part on consumers’ understanding
and acting on objective climate risk information. Yet such information is not interpreted in
isolation. Interpretation may be influenced by immediate contextual cues. This research examines
how weather conditions, as one example of relevant contextual cues, influence consumers’
responses to property-level climate risk information. Pairing website visit data from an online
platform providing flood risk information with the weather data at users’ location, we demonstrate
that weather is associated with interest in personal climate-hazard risk. Specifically, visits to the
website increase following periods of rainfall and decline during extended dry spells at the users’
locations. Beyond generating interest in climate-hazard risks, we show in four experiments that
weather moderates the effect of objective climate-hazard risk on consumers’ judgments. When
weather conditions contradict the objective risk, consumers’ judgments shift away from the direction
implied by the objective risk information. In contrast, when weather aligns with the objective
risk, weather effects are mostly absent. These effects also trickle down to consumers’ willingness
to adopt protective measures. These findings advance our understanding of consumers’ evaluation
of risks by showing that heterogeneity in risk perception and protection motivation can emerge
from an asymmetric integration of objective risk information and immediate contextual cues depending
on whether the signals align or not.

articles.title: Conspiratorial mentality among older people: The role of loneliness, depression, anxiety, and social media use
articles.authors: Michal Mužík; Jan Serek
articles.abstract: Despite age being a significant sociodemographic correlate of conspiratorial mentality, surprisingly little is known about its precursors and consequences among older people. Older people are often considered at risk of psychological distress, which often relates to conspiratorial mentality. Our study therefore assumed bidirectional relations between these constructs. Distress was represented by loneliness, anxiety, and depression. We also investigated potential moderation by social media use, as conspiracy theories tend to be disseminated on such media. We tested these associations linearly and quadratically using data from a two-wave longitudinal study of Czech adults aged 60+ (NW1 = 4133, MageW1 = 69.1). Conspiratorial mentality was not predicted by other variables, indicating that these are probably not risk factors for such mentality. Conversely, conspiratorial mentality positively predicted only anxiety. Social media use moderation and quadratic effects were unsupported. Overall, the study suggests that conspiratorial mentality can be an anxiety-provoking experience among older people.

articles.title: Relational Mobility and the Sharing of Positive and Negative Reputation Across Societies
articles.authors: Haruno Kusakabe; Masaki Yuki
articles.abstract: The sharing and use of reputational information about others are fundamental to human societies. Yet little is known about how the sharing of positive and negative reputational information varies across socio-ecological conditions. We examined its associations with relational mobility, a socio-ecological factor pertaining to the freedom and opportunity to form and select interpersonal relationships. Across three surveys in the United States and Japan (total N = 930), participants reported perceived prevalence of positive and negative reputational information in their local social environments. In Study 2, they also reported their own everyday sharing. For positive information, US participants reported a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing than Japanese participants, and within-country associations with relational mobility generally supported our predictions. For negative information, within-country associations were generally negative, as predicted, but country differences were either nonsignificant or opposite to the predicted direction. Indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were consistent with our predictions for both positive and negative information across studies. These findings highlight the importance of considering both socio-ecological context and reputational valence in research on reputation.

articles.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles.title: 42 Days of Summer: A diary study of awe
articles.authors: Valerie van Mulukom; Mari van Emmerik; Victoria Lorrimar
articles.abstract: Awe has long been associated with religious experience, but it may also offer nonreligious individuals a route to meaning, connection, and transcendence. Most research has, however, relied on laboratory inductions and has treated awe as a single experience. We conducted a pre-registered six-week diary study with 200 nonreligious British adults over the summer holidays, distinguishing three types of awe: transformative awe (being in the presence of something vast and mysterious that transcends one's understanding of the world), amazement awe, and reverential awe. Over the summer, 78.8% of participants reported at least one amazement awe experience, 51.5% at least one reverential awe experience, and 20.6% at least one transformative awe experience. The types differed in their contexts and phenomenology. Nature was the most common context for all three, but transformative awe was more often related to space and religious, spiritual, or mystical experiences, and reverential awe to moral beauty and experiences with close ones. Transformative awe was the most intense, followed by amazement and reverential awe. Most experiences were rated as not at all religious (90.0%), but over half were rated as at least somewhat spiritual (52.5%). The frequency and extent of awe did not predict changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality from before to after the summer. In exploratory analyses, the amazement rating of participants’ most awe-inspiring experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing. These findings suggest that awe is not a single experience, and that nonreligious individuals frequently experience awe as spiritual but not religious.

articles.title: Just-in-Time Neuromodulation: A Precision, State-Dependent Paradigm for On-Demand Brain Intervention
articles.authors: Ashkan Rashedi; Aref Pariz; Jing Jin; Marzieh Zare; ANDRE RUSSOWSKY BRUNONI; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles.abstract: Neuromodulation is commonly delivered on fixed schedules, whereas psychiatric and neurological symptoms fluctuate over time. Just-in-Time Neuromodulation (JiT-NM) offers a framework for aligning intervention with the emergence or escalation of clinically relevant neural or symptomatic states. We propose three essential components: targeting the desired state, a state-detection system, and a neuromodulatory intervention capable of acting within a clinically useful time window. A fourth, optional component, adaptive personalization, may refine detection models and stimulation parameters over time. JiT-NM may support self-initiated or autonomous delivery, open-loop or closed-loop control, informed by automated symptom recognition or self-report, physiological signals, digital phenotyping, or wearable neural sensing. Established responsive and adaptive implanted stimulation systems provide clinical precedents, while early investigations in psychiatric disorders support further exploration. We discuss how neuroimaging-derived targets and biomarkers might be translated into compact, individualized sensing-and-stimulation systems, emphasizing the need to validate reliable state detection with fewer sensors. Key challenges include demonstrating the added value of intervention timing, accommodating changing neural dynamics, establishing real-world usability, as well as addressing safety, privacy, and regulatory requirements. JiT-NM provides a framework for investigating whether on-demand, state-based stimulation can complement scheduled treatment or achieve superior outcomes while reducing unnecessary treatment burden.

articles.title: Reframing Educational Value in EdTech for Neuro-Inclusive Primary School Classrooms: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sonja Tervola; Emily J. Goodacre; Jenny Louise Gibson
articles.abstract: Educational technologies (EdTech) are increasingly used to support neurodivergent learners in primary classrooms, yet their educational value remains difficult to establish across diverse learners, technologies, and contexts. We address this challenge through a scoping review of EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms, screening 3,340 records across six research databases and including 93 studies. The findings reveal an uneven evidence base, concentrated on autistic learners, individualised academic and cognitive support, and emerging technologies such as virtual reality, robotics, and artificial intelligence, while social, communicative, and peer-interaction outcomes received less attention. Design and evaluation processes were frequently researcher-led or unreported, with limited participation from children and other stakeholders. Intended goals and evaluated outcomes were often misaligned, and educational value was predominantly validated by researchers rather than by those using the technologies in classrooms. Building on these findings, we argue that educational value is constructed across three interconnected dimensions: conceptual (what counts as valuable), operational (how value is measured), and endorsed (whose judgements validate it). When these dimensions are disconnected, claims of educational value can become detached from the priorities and experiences of those the technologies are intended to serve. In response, we propose two complementary frameworks: one to guide future EdTech research and development, and another to help practitioners assess the educational value and relevance of EdTech for their classrooms.

articles.title: How Does Profile Text Signal Desirability in Online Dating? A Meta-Analysis of Cue Valence and Explicitness
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Signaling mate desirability is central to a well-functioning online dating market. This meta-analysis examines how profile text signals the owner's desirability. Drawing on research on negativity and cue diagnosticity, warranting theory, and signaling theory, I test how the valence (positive vs. negative) and explicitness (explicit vs. implicit) of text-based cues shape viewers' reactions. I analyzed 13 experiments (53 effect sizes) drawn from a scoping review of online dating research. Text-based cues have a small, heterogeneous effect on evaluations, dating intentions, and behavior toward the profile owner (g = 0.25). Negative cues move responses (g = 0.38), whereas positive cues do not (g = −0.07). Explicit and implicit cues do not differ overall, but the gap between negative and positive cues is larger for explicit cues. The results show that strategic verbal content in online dating profiles works as a screening device, carrying meaningful information about undesirable traits in a partner.

articles.title: Changing moral beliefs and behaviors using human-AI dialogues
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Carter Allen; Lucius Caviola; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Moral beliefs are widely considered resistant to change, yet the rise of conversational AI offers new tools for moral persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N = 500) in which participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them that either eating meat, or not giving to charity, is morally wrong. Conversations produced large and immediate shifts in moral beliefs in the intended direction (Cohen’s d = 0.37–0.48), along with corresponding behavioral effects: participants in the charity conversation condition donated 16.35% more of their bonus money to charity than participants in the meat conversation condition, while those in the meat conversation condition were 25.04 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher compared to those in the charity conversation condition. One month later, the effect on burger voucher choice remained significant, while other effects did not. NLP analysis of participant moral justifications and AI persuasive strategies suggests that moral persuasion was partly driven by factual correction—particularly in the meat domain, where factual appeals to the naturalness and biological necessity of meat eating were the most common among participants—alongside direct moral argumentation. These results demonstrate that human-AI dialogues can produce meaningful change in moral beliefs and behavior, raising important questions about the capacity of conversational AI to shape human values at scale.

articles.title: Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas & Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models
articles.authors: Joao F Guassi Moreira; Jared Block; Alondra M. Cruz; Craig K. Enders; Amanda Kay Montoya
articles.abstract: The use of multilevel models in behavioral and social sciences has risen dramatically in the past several decades. Researchers using these models often consult highly-referenced simulation studies when designing their own studies, especially for sample-size planning.However, current literature suggests two issues with this practice. First, recent efforts to replicate findings from seminal simulation studies suggest the rate of replicability is far from ideal (Luijken et al., 2024). Second, researchers are now using more complex models but foundational simulation studies were conducted under much simpler conditions. To address these two issues, we propose a replication and extension of Maas & Hox (2005), a widely cited study that recommended Level-2 sample sizes of N = 50 to be sufficient under specific conditions. We replicate their core findings and propose several extensions based on a literature search of multilevel modeling practices employed in fifty recent studies.These extensions include examining conditions with imbalanced data across higher-level units, varying the number of random slopes and cross-level interactions, and varying effect sizes. These results could ensure the existing literature relies on a replicable simulation study while also informing multilevel study planning for complex models which are becoming increasingly popular in behavioral and social sciences.

articles.title: REPAIR: Random-effect prediction adjustment for inference in regression
articles.authors: Zachary Andrew Vig; Michael N. Hallquist
articles.abstract: Random-effect predictions from multilevel models are often used to relate individual differences in processes, such as growth or stress reactivity, to other variables. Yet, regressions using these predictions can distort regression coefficients and standard errors because the predictions combine shrinkage with sampling error. Here, we introduce and evaluate Random-Effect Prediction Adjustment for Inference in Regression (REPAIR), a two-step framework for linear regressions involving random effects. For linear Gaussian multilevel models, REPAIR obtains likelihood-only predictions by generalized least squares. A regularized method-of-moments estimator then uses estimated cluster-specific sampling-error covariances to correct structural moments. Four simulation studies examined random effects as predictors, outcomes, or both, including unequal cluster sizes. REPAIR generally showed small bias at medium to high predictor reliability and often had lower root mean squared error than alternative methods. Low predictor reliability remained challenging, particularly for confidence interval coverage in small samples. These findings support REPAIR as a practical framework for estimating structural relationships involving random effects while accounting for their measurement uncertainty.

articles.title: Young Life Evaluation in Decline: A Case Study of Norway
articles.authors: August Nilsson; Karoline Kopperud; Espen Røysamb; Tim Lomas; Lyle H Ungar; Ragnhild Bang Nes
articles.abstract: In 73% of the world’s countries, adults under 30 years of age report the highest life evaluation (i.e., happiness). A notable exception has emerged in North America and Northern Europe, where this pattern has reversed, with older adults reporting greater life evaluation than the young. We analyzed Gallup World Poll data from 2006–2024, covering 2.6 million respondents worldwide and 16,009 in Norway, to examine shifts in the age gap in life evaluation and their determinants. Norway is a particularly valuable case for illustrating this reversal: since ranking as the world’s happiest country in 2017, it has declined in both absolute terms and relative rankings, with national statistics revealing a pronounced well-being gap between young and old. We found that the decline in life evaluation scores in Norway largely reflects decreasing scores among young adults (18-30 years), whose scores have dropped significantly since 2017 (p < .001; d = 0.37) and are now markedly lower than those of older adults (p < .001; d = 0.41). We further confirmed that this trend is limited to a small set of countries; of all 2,508 linear correlations between age and life evaluation in different countries, 83% were negative, and only 2% were r > .10, which was the case in Norway 2022–2024. We examined potential explanations of the observed change in Norway. Only a few of the 70 variables in the Gallup World Poll seem potentially relevant for the increased age difference in life evaluations in Norway. Across multiple analyses we find the most important variables are i) stress-related factors (e.g., feeling well-rested and stress), and ii) economic standards (e.g., standard of living satisfaction and household income satisfaction). The study emphasizes the imperative for highly developed countries to prioritise the well-being of their young despite overall prosperity and high living standards.

articles.title: “Treat us as capable”: Neurodivergent youths’ perceptions on adult support in digital participation
articles.authors: Yvette Edelaar-Peeters; Rogier de Groot; I. Chaplinska; Sophie Mary; H.M. Koning Ina; Peter Nikken; Carlo Schuengel; Hendrien Lourine Kaal
articles.abstract: Digital participation is essential for neurodivergent youth. However, parents, teachers, and professionals often struggle to provide appropriate digital support. Like offline contexts, supporting neurodivergent youths’ online behaviors requires finding a balance between protection from potential risks and the promotion of autonomy and empowerment. Until now, scholars have predominantly focused on caregivers' perspectives. Therefore, in this study perceptions of these youngsters themselves are investigated. Survey data of 58 neurodivergent youth on experienced digital support were analyzed. Responses supported the distinction between enabling-authoritative support and restrictive-authoritarian support. Neurodivergent youth reported that parents and teachers more often applied enabling-authoritative support and indicated that they found this approach more effective. These findings underscore the importance of enabling rather than restrictive digital support also for neurodivergent youth, as digitalization opens up new opportunities for redressing their inequities in participation.

articles.title: Relational Calibration: A Framework for Dynamic Instructional Regulation in Complex Learning Environments
articles.authors: Delwin B. Carter
articles.abstract: Relational Calibration (RC) is a theoretical framework for organizing enacted instructor responses during ongoing instruction. It specifies three response dimensions: relational positioning, instructional posture, and real-time modulation. Interpersonal attunement coordinates these dimensions by linking emerging instructional evidence and its interpretation to enacted responses. The framework’s functional target is sustaining engagement with demanding intellectual work while preserving intellectual demand. Grounded in research on professional noticing, adaptive and responsive teaching, contingent scaffolding, interpersonal teacher behavior, relational competence, and instructional communication, RC brings relational, instructional, and expressive aspects of response into a common event-level representation. It distinguishes observable evidence, interpretation, enacted response, instructional architecture, the functional target, proposed mechanisms, subsequent outcomes, and measurement. These distinctions provide a basis for examining how instructors coordinate responses within particular instructional events and how those responses relate to engagement and preserved demand. The manuscript develops the framework’s theoretical foundations, dimensions, and coordinating process, then specifies a measurement and research agenda addressing event boundaries, response coding, independent criterion measurement, comparison with established frameworks, and enactment across instructional contexts.

articles.title: Neurodivergent Youth Online: Professional Needs, Capacities, and Challenges
articles.authors: Yvette Edelaar-Peeters; Rogier de Groot; I. Chaplinska; Sophie Mary; H.M. Koning Ina; Peter Nikken; Carlo Schuengel; Hendrien Lourine Kaal
articles.abstract: Healthcare professionals and educators have expressed a need for greater support in guiding neurodivergent youth in their digital lives. Professionals’ perceptions of the digital needs, opportunities, and risks of neurodivergent youth, and how these perceptions are translated into their own needs for support, using a mixed-methods design consisting of online questionnaires and focus group interviews was studied.  Key support needs included collaboration with parents, navigating professional responsibilities, and addressing the gap between digital knowledge and online behaviour.

articles.title: Reputational Concern Across Cultures
articles.authors: Ivan Deschenaux; Poorvi Kumar Iyer; Cody T. Ross; Sarah Alami; Komal Chauhan; Werner Hertzog; Edmond Seabright; Eleanor A. Power
articles.abstract:
We conduct experimental economic games designed to study how reputational concern influences people's economic decisions. Donors make a series of ``Dictator Game'' decisions, splitting an endowment between themselves and a recipient. Crucially, recipients are not anonymous strangers, but are other individuals from the same community as the donor, presented to donors via photographs. By varying the identity of the recipient and whether or not the recipient will come to know the identity of the donor, we can effectively vary the reputational stake of the donor's decision. We expect that when Dictator Game allocation decisions have greater reputational stakes, donors will be more generous.
Greater reputational stakes could arise from: the revelation of the donor's identity, the social proximity of donor and recipient, and the general network position of donor and recipient, all of which we consider. We conduct these games in eight rural communities in five countries, where we already have full sociodemographic and social network data on players and their connections. While there is substantial cross-site variation in the amounts given, we find strikingly similar effects of revelation and social proximity on allocation decisions: in all sites, donors give only slightly more in contexts where their identity is revealed, as opposed to being kept anonymous. Whether anonymous or revealed, donors give appreciably less to recipients who are more socially distant, with the largest drop occurring between immediate connections and connections-of-connections. We find mixed evidence that the effect of revealing a donor's identity diminishes with social distance. Finally, we do not find clear effects for the network position of donor and recipient. These results improve our understanding of how economic behaviour is intertwined with reputational dynamics in a wide variety of contexts. While altruistic behaviour does increase with reputational concern cross-culturally, it also appears that in tight-knit, small communities, absence of reputational concern may, contra expectations, lead only to a small increase in selfishness.

articles.title: Does Acquiescence Bias Distort Measurement Invariance Across Multiple Groups? A Monte Carlo Comparison of Tree-Based Factor Analytic Methods
articles.authors: Tugay Kaçak; David Navarro González
articles.abstract: Acquiescence (ACQ), the tendency to agree regardless of item content, can differ across groups and thereby mimic or mask measurement non-invariance. Model-based recursive partitioning (MOB) combined with factor-analytic models (e.g. EFAtree, CFAtree) is increasingly used to detect non-invariance across many covariates, but whether the detected heterogeneity can be attributed to its correct source is unknown. In a Monte Carlo simulation (432 conditions, 500 replications each), we compared EFAtree and CFAtree with their random-intercept (RI) versions under four data-generating conditions: groups differed in neither source, in ACQ only, in the content loadings only, or in both. We also propose a block-wise efficient score test that separates instability in the RI variance from instability in the content loadings by projecting out all other parameters. All trees held the nominal Type I error rate. When groups differed only in ACQ, trees without an RI factor mistook the difference for metric non-invariance under unbalanced keying or missed it under balanced keying, whereas the RI trees detected it regardless of keying. Applied to the true grouping variable, the standard block test, which selects a block from the fully decorrelated scores, attributed purely substantive non-invariance to ACQ in 79% of replications, more often in larger samples. The efficient test kept this misattribution near the nominal level (.06) and attributed heterogeneity correctly at the attainable maximum. With one content factor, EFA- and CFA-based trees produced identical results. In an empirical example with the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (N = 26236), the RI variance differed across countries but not across age groups or genders, and even across countries it was only one of several unstable parameter blocks, alongside the intercepts and the factor-mean and factor-variance directions. Before a split is interpreted as measurement non-invariance, its source should be examined with an RI factor and efficient block-wise tests.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Low-Vision Navigation Reveals Shortcomings of Current Navigation Frameworks: Proposals for Experiments and Design
articles.authors: Jack Morris; Bastien Perroy; Roberto Casati
articles.abstract: People with low vision (PLVs) experience difficulties in spatial navigation associated with their low vision (LV) and are inadequately supported by status quo information solutions. The LV case, in which visual input is present but functionally unreliable, also falls out of scope of existing taxonomies of spatial navigation derived from mostly normally sighted subjects. We propose three perturbations through which LV adds attentional demands to navigation: we review evidence that it de-automates the task of avoiding obstacles and safely walking (vigilant locomotion), hypothesize that it strains visual search by creating uncertainty about information sources’ presence, placement, form, and accessibility (naive search), and conjecture that it lowers confidence for wayfinding decisions, encouraging backtracking and frequent confirmation (fragile decisions). Empirical evidence supports that vigilant locomotion under LV interferes with concurrent cognitive processes, especially spatial learning. We hypothesize that this interference extends to wayfinding and that difficulties in information sampling (naive search) and low metacognitive confidence (fragile decisions) additionally strain attention. Accordingly, we introduce three design aims which can help evaluate whether current and prospective wayfinding information solutions support low-vision navigation by addressing these perturbations; information should be continuous at step-level, easy to sample, and confirmatory via paired feedback. Future research should directly test these predictions in ecological contexts and investigate the possibility that acute stressors can mimic the LV-related perturbations in the general population.

articles.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics.
articles.authors: Tyler Kwan; Orestis Zavlis; Caroline Selai; Michael Moutoussis
articles.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

articles.title: Persona Diversity and Error Structure in LLM Crowds
articles.authors: Itsuki Fujisaki
articles.abstract: Can psychologically different roles make a crowd of large language model responses more accurate? We examined demographic personas, cognitive personas, and instructions inspired by the wisdom of the inner crowd. An exploratory reanalysis used six conditions on 15 MARBLES estimation items presented as text or with photographs. We calculated error after aggregating responses and distinguished two comparisons: role-based crowds against neutral responses of the same number, and heterogeneous against homogeneous crowds reconstructed from the same response pools. For text, the 12-response stacked condition had lower mean relative absolute error than a matched hierarchical neutral control, 0.766825 versus 0.958008. The difference was −0.191183, with a 95% item-bootstrap interval of [−0.518117, 0.015682], and one item accounted for much of the mean advantage. The corresponding image difference was −0.004316 [−0.026710, 0.019478]. Within the same response pools, composition effects were generally small and depended on the comparison and error measure. Image responses frequently underestimated the true quantities, while persona error patterns were highly correlated in both presentations. A supplementary Fermi analysis documents how rounding changed an earlier condition ranking. These findings distinguish changes associated with role-based prompting from the additional value of combining different roles, and identify the error structure that each comparison can assess.

articles.title: Multiparty conversation predominates in children's language environments across diverse cultural settings
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Little is known about the dynamics of children’s conversations outside of urban Western contexts, where research focuses on one-on-one interactions with parents. Our study addresses this gap, aggregating naturalistic speech data gathered in 10 countries across multiple labs, and using novel speech diarization algorithms to extract and classify different types of conversation. We analyzed 23,000 hours of child-centered audio recordings taken from 844 children (mean age 23 months; 389 girls) across urban, agricultural, and foraging societies. We found that multiparty conversations, involving at least three speakers, are more frequent than any other type of conversation. Across settings, children’s relative exposure to conversation differed based on their age, number of siblings, and mother’s education. We conclude that the kinds of conversation most often studied differ from those children typically encounter. Greater focus on children’s conversations in multiparty contexts may provide a more representative picture of their daily experience with language.

articles_hidden.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles_hidden.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles_hidden.title: Failure to distinguish “mental health” from “mental illness” disrupts effective policy for population well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Hannes Jarke; Sofia Pelica
articles_hidden.abstract: The semantics and measurement of “mental health”, “well-being”, and “mental illness” have long been debated - as has the way clinicians and policymakers are expected to respond to their associated insights. However, despite existing discussion on distinctions between these terms, there is an urgent need to more forcefully articulate how key terminology in mental health should be used. Failures to do so have been problematic and directly impacted how mental health is understood, which has subsequently impacted efforts to prevent and treat mental illness as well as protect and promote mental health. Here we highlight significant concerns about incorrect use of these terms, their implications, and why the field needs to urgently apply more stringency in the literature. Our aim is not to criticize journals, articles, or authors for such mixing, but rather to provide compelling arguments as to why it is critical to be correct and precise about how these are discussed, measured, and addressed to benefit population well-being.

articles_hidden.title: The Dark Triad and trait aggression in women and men: Clarifying the substantive consequences of factor overlap
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolás González-Raposo; Pablo Polo; Eduardo Galaz Villarroel; Katrin Schaefer; Bernhard Fink; Todd K. Shackelford; Virgil Zeigler-Hill; Tobias Koch; Ulrich S. Tran; Jose Antonio Muñoz Reyes
articles_hidden.abstract: Although the Dark Triad (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) has been consistently linked to aggressive behaviors such as bullying and violence, two important questions about these associations remain unresolved. First, little is known about how they differ between women and men. Second, it remains unclear how factor overlap affects their substantive interpretation. Drawing on evolutionary accounts of intrasexual competition, we predict stronger associations with physical and verbal aggression in men and hostility in women. We test these predictions on Short Dark Triad and Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire data from 600 Chilean adults, using bifactor (S−1) structural equation modeling. We find that Machiavellianism predicts all aggression outcomes, psychopathy-specific variance positively predicts physical aggression, and narcissism-specific variance negatively predicts hostility. Sex differences in aggression overlap with sex differences in aversive traits, but none of the Dark Triad-aggression associations consistently differ by sex. By introducing the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE), we provide the first substantive translation of these bifactor associations. VWLE clarifies how reference facet and trait-specific associations reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism, making the implications of residual coefficients explicit.

articles_hidden.title: Menstrual Cycle Status and the Acute Subjective Psychedelic Experience
articles_hidden.authors: Alaina Srivastav; Sunjuri Sun; Peter Hendricks; Walter Osika; Cecilia Ulrika Dagsdotter Stenfors; Sankalp Chaturvedi; Michelle Olofsson; Gabriella Smedfors; Simon Goldberg; Otto Simonsson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Individual differences shape the acute subjective psychedelic experience, but menstrual cycle status remains an understudied source of potential variability.
Methods: In a longitudinal observational study, 169 participants reported psychedelic use during the two-month study period. Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69). Primary analyses examined associations between cycle status and ego dissolution (Ego Dissolution Inventory; EDI), mystical-type experience (Mystical Experience Questionnaire; MEQ), and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire; CEQ), adjusting for dose and age. Exploratory analyses examined MEQ and CEQ subscales and post-acute risk of harm to self and others.
Results: Participants menstruating during their experience reported higher EDI scores than both those menstruating but not during the experience and male participants (β=−0.89 and −0.68, ps≤.011). Cycle status was not associated with MEQ or CEQ scores. Exploratory analyses found higher physical distress and death subscale scores among participants menstruating during their experience than among those menstruating but not during the experience (β=−0.77 and −0.80, ps≤.005). Risk of post-acute harm to self and others was higher among those menstruating during the experience than among those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (OR=6.41, p=.022).
Conclusions: Menstrual cycle timing may be associated with aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, specifically ego dissolution and potentially risk of post-acute harm to self and others. These preliminary findings support further investigation of menstrual cycle status in psychedelic research.

articles_hidden.title: Gender-Inclusive Voice and Communication Training: Supporting Nonbinary Clients
articles_hidden.authors: Maura Philippone; Thea Knowles; Becks von Duering
articles_hidden.abstract: Nonbinary clients may pursue gender-affirming voice training (GAVT) goals that extend beyond traditional masculinization and feminization goals. This clinical perspective discusses potential applications of existing clinical frameworks for nonbinary clients, with particular focus on meta-therapy and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) as gender-inclusive approaches. These approaches support gender-inclusive, person-centered exploration of voice and communication characteristics while drawing on established principles of speech production. Although further research is needed to establish more gender-inclusive acoustic and perceptual outcome measures, clinicians can presently use customizable, person-centered approaches to support diverse GAVT goals and provide affirming care.

articles_hidden.title: SaccadeJS: Webcam eye tracking for behavioral experiments in a web browser
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua R de Leeuw; Colin Mikulski; Alex Teabo; Cherrie Chang
