articles_hidden.abstract: Webcam eye tracking allows researchers to study eye movements in large, geographically diverse online samples, but its accuracy has limited it to coarse comparisons, such as which half or quadrant of the screen a participant is looking at. We introduce SaccadeJS, an open-source webcam eye tracker that runs entirely in the participant's browser. SaccadeJS uses a neural network to transform images of the eyes to features, which a ridge regression maps to screen positions. The network can be rapidly calibrated by computing new regression weights on a sample of fixations at known locations. To train the model, we collected a new dataset of 2,003 participants who fixated targets on their own laptop and desktop computers. In a validation study with 200 new online participants, the median participant's error was about 4% of the screen diagonal. That accuracy is enough to distinguish many more, and smaller, areas of interest than halves and quadrants. We also developed a timing calibration routine to measure each participant's camera lag. After correction, saccade latencies matched distributions from laboratory experiments. We report how different calibration strategies and image characteristics affect accuracy. SaccadeJS could be run in real time on about one third of the participants in the validation study; for others, the library processes frames in the background while the experiment runs. SaccadeJS can be used as standalone software for webcam eye tracking or in conjunction with jsPsych through a set of provided plugins for calibration, validation, and recording.

articles_hidden.title: The control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Georg Keller; Philipp Sterzer
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the last half century, we have made little progress in the treatment of schizophrenia. A key contributor to this is an insufficient understanding of what is causing the disorder. There are currently two broad families of hypotheses: those focused on a dopaminergic dysfunction, and those focused on a glutamatergic dysfunction. Based on recent findings that antipsychotic drugs exhibit cell-type specific and long-term effects on cortical circuit function, we integrate the two hypotheses into what we call the control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia. It builds on the assumption that schizophrenia is the result of a developmental miswiring of cortical circuits that is based on glutamatergic dysfunction and causes aberrant cortical activity dynamics. These cortical alterations likely underlie cognitive dysfunction, one of the core treatment-resistant symptoms of schizophrenia. The control limit hypothesis further postulates that the brain responds to and can partially mitigate these aberrant cortical dynamics by increasing dopamine levels in the striatum. When this regulatory system is driven to a control limit and dopamine levels exceed a given threshold, psychosis emerges. Beyond explaining much of the existing data, the hypothesis makes several predictions about cortical function testable in mice and humans.

articles_hidden.title: (Phon)aesthetics Beyond Sound: Sociocultural Associations, Aesthetic Appeal, and Perceived Valence in Sign Languages
articles_hidden.authors: Theresa Matzinger; Monika Boruta-Żywiczyńska
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aesthetic evaluations of languages depend not only on the linguistic signal but also on
language-external factors, notably familiarity with a language and the sociocultural
associations triggered by recognising it. For spoken languages, these factors are hard to
separate, because languages evoking strong cultural associations are usually also familiar. We
used sign languages to isolate the influence of sociocultural associations, testing hearing nonsigners
who were unfamiliar with American (ASL) and French (LSF) Sign Language but
familiar with the associated cultures. Participants rated 64 signs (32 ASL, 32 LSF; half
positively, half negatively valenced) for aesthetic appeal, perceived valence and, once given
the meaning, perceived iconicity. Half of participants were told which language each sign
belonged to, whereas the other half received no such information. Appeal ratings for ASL and
LSF differed only when the languages were indicated: the more participants liked French
relative to US-American culture, the more appealing they found LSF relative to ASL, and vice
versa. No such pattern emerged without this information. Sociocultural associations can thus
shape aesthetic evaluation of a language independently of direct linguistic experience.
Additionally, although participants did not know the signs’ meanings, positively valenced signs
were rated as more positive and, particularly in ASL, more appealing than negatively valenced
signs. This suggests that aesthetic and affective evaluations of signs are closely linked. Finally,
more iconic signs received valence ratings more closely aligned with their actual valence. To
our knowledge, this is the first extension of (phon)aesthetic research to sign languages.

articles_hidden.title: Neural responses to socioemotional information are more similar among siblings and relate to social competence
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Scatolin; Elena Federici; Plamina Dimanova; Dennis Saikkonen; Jonathan Bugmann; Nora Maria Raschle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Socioemotional skills are fundamental to children’s well-being and development, yet the
neurodevelopmental processes through which familial relationships contribute to these skills
remain poorly understood. While socioemotional skills are partly heritable, they are also shaped by
social learning through interactions with others, including siblings. Sibling relationships represent
one of the earliest and most enduring social contexts throughout development and provide a
valuable context for investigating how familial relatedness is reflected in children's neural
processing of socioemotional information. However, little is known about whether siblings exhibit
similarities in these neural responses and how such similarities relate to socioemotional behavior.
In this study, we investigated whether sibling dyads show greater similarity in neural responses
during socioemotional processing than unrelated child dyads and whether such neural similarity is
associated with socioemotional functioning. To assess this, 120 children (6-14 years), including 39
sibling dyads, completed a naturalistic fMRI movie-watching task designed to elicit socioemotional
responses. Results showed that sibling dyads exhibited greater whole-brain functional neural
similarity during socioemotional processing than unrelated children across the whole brain. Region-
of-interest analyses further revealed greater functional neural similarity among siblings across
several prefrontal, temporal, and limbic regions, including the left ventromedial prefrontal cortex
(vmPFC). Moreover, greater similarity in left vmPFC responses, a region implicated in social
cognition, was associated with higher levels of socially competent behavior in both sibling and
unrelated dyads, suggesting that neural similarity may be particularly pronounced among children
with higher social competence. These findings highlight sibling relationships as an informative
context for investigating familial similarities in neural responses to socioemotional information and
their associations with socioemotional behavior during childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Getting ready for minority language transmission: Language management preparation among expecting parents in Fryslân
articles_hidden.authors: Suzanne Victoria Dekker; Jelske Dijkstra; Pavlina Heinzova; Mirjam Vellinga; Ruth Kircher
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines a previously unexplored aspect of family language policies: namely how expecting parents prepare for language management, focusing on their engagement with language-related resources – books, leaflets, magazines, etc. – to support them in getting ready to raise their children (bi-/multilingually) with a minority language. The majority language of the Netherlands is Dutch; Fryslân is home to most speakers of the minority language Frisian. Findings show that most participants decided what language(s) to transmit prior to pregnancy. Furthermore,  expecting parents who ultimately ended up transmitting Frisian were more aware of, and used more, resources than parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian. The former also indicated a desire for additional resources to support bilingual (Dutch-Frisian) child-rearing and Frisian transmission. The paper discusses the study’s implications for policy and planning aiming to promote the intergenerational transmission of Frisian, and thereby promoting its maintenance and revitalisation.

articles_hidden.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles_hidden.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Musical Mood Regulation for Efficacy Beliefs and Hope in the Climate Crisis
articles_hidden.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Climate change is associated with a range of emotional responses, yet little is known about 
the role of music in regulating climate-related emotions and supporting adaptive 
psychological outcomes. Because music is widely used to regulate emotions and can foster 
positive affect, emotional coping, and resilience, it may also help individuals maintain hope 
when confronting the challenges of climate change. The present study examined whether 
music-based mood regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this 
relationship is mediated by climate efficacy beliefs. A cross-sectional online survey was 
completed by 310 adults. Participants reported their use of music to regulate climate-
related emotions, climate efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective 
efficacy, and collective outcome expectancy), and hope. Relationships among the variables 
were examined using correlation analyses and structural equation modeling. Several music-
based regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, 
were positively associated with hope. Some regulation strategies were also positively 
associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, 
whereas no significant bivariate associations emerged with collective efficacy. Structural 
equation modeling indicated a significant total indirect effect of music-based regulation on 
hope through climate efficacy beliefs. However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy 
emerged as significant mediators. Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy 
did not significantly mediate the association. The direct association between music-based 
regulation and hope remained significant, indicating partial mediation. These findings 
suggest that individuals who use music to regulate climate-related emotions report greater 
hope and that this association is partly explained by stronger perceptions of personal and 
collective capability. Climate efficacy beliefs emerged as a small yet significant pathway 
linking music-based regulation and hope. Music may therefore represent an accessible 
everyday resource that supports adaptive engagement with climate emotions and fosters 
hope in the context of climate change.

articles_hidden.title: Reading from childhood to adolescence: enduring influences of home environment on behaviour, motivation and proficiency
articles_hidden.authors: Sanne W van der Kleij; Jessie Ricketts; Laura Shapiro
articles_hidden.abstract: According to theoretical models of reading engagement, reading behaviours and reading motivation both influence reading proficiency. Additionally, annual surveys of young people’s reading engagement show decreasing numbers of children who report enjoying reading over time and across ages, but we lack longitudinal evidence confirming this decline. Data from a longitudinal study in [Blinded], UK (n = 598, 285 girls) were used to model the influence of HLE, reading motivation and reading behaviour on reading comprehension skills. Reading motivation, reading behaviour (i.e. time spent reading) and reading comprehension were assessed from age 10 to 15 and HLE was assessed in a subsample at age 11 (n = 299). Growth models showed that reading motivation and time spent reading declined from 11 to 13 years and then stabilised from age 14-15. However, trajectories of change differed across sex and socioeconomic status. In mediation models, the home literacy environment at age 11 was associated with children’s own reading engagement and showed direct and indirect associations with children’s reading comprehension outcomes. Our findings highlight the crucial influence of reading motivation on reading outcomes and uncover a longer-term role of HLE than previously assumed, extending well beyond childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Goals, Predictions, Valence: A Model Comparison of Agency Emergence
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas Richter; Marcel Raphael Schreiner
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of agency (SoA), our feeling of control over actions and their environmental effects, has been explained through different theoretical models. This study compares three: the comparator model, proposing that SoA emerges from matching motor-based predictions to perceptual feedback, the ideomotor model, proposing that SoA emerges from monitoring goal achievement, and a self-serving bias model, proposing that SoA reflects self-attribution of positive and external attribution of negative outcomes. Participants performed a target-hitting task with manipulated visual feedback of positive or negative valence and rated their SoA on a subset of trials. The three models predict different SoA patterns based on motor activity appropriateness, goal achievement, and outcome valence. The ideomotor model best fit the empirical data, outperforming both alternatives, whereas evidence for an additional effect of outcome valence was ambiguous. These findings question the dominant role of motor-based predictions in SoA emergence and highlight goal achievement as a key determinant of SoA.

articles_hidden.title: A Bi-Factor Generalized Cognitive Diagnosis Model Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Rodrigo Schames Kreitchmann; Pablo Nájera; Francisco José Abad
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) are often applied to constructs that are largely unidimensional in nature (e.g., mathematics, reading, mental health status) where a set of discrete attributes coexists with a dominant general proficiency dimension. This article presents the bi-factor CDM model (BF-CDM), which partitions item responses into a direct effect of continuous general proficiency and a discrete attribute-mastery tier, allowing mastery classifications to be made beyond what is attributable to general ability. By modeling both tiers explicitly, the BF-CDM makes it possible to evaluate the contribution of the discrete tier itself. Specifically, it can show whether the hypothesized attributes carry diagnostic information beyond general proficiency, both through model comparison with the nested unidimensional model and through the reliability of the attribute-specific component. A simulation study manipulating sample size, test length, number of attributes, and attribute-tier discrimination shows accurate recovery of item and person parameters, and of the model-implied response functions. An application to reading comprehension data from PISA illustrates the practical value of the model: reliability of attribute-mastery classifications drops substantially once variance attributable to general proficiency is partialled out, indicating that much of the apparent diagnostic precision obtained under a saturated attribute structure reflects a single dominant general factor.

articles_hidden.title: Does Teacher Praise Make Children Feel Less Smart? Two Preregistered Virtual Reality Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Lena-Emilia Schenker; Jellie Sierksma; Milica Nikolic; Eddie Brummelman
articles_hidden.abstract: Does teacher praise make children feel less smart? When two students perform equally, teachers might praise the student they believe worked harder, implicitly conveying to that student that they have lower ability. We tested this hypothesis through two preregistered experiments in a novel Virtual Reality classroom with children aged 7-13 (Study 1: N = 212, Study 2: N = 225). After the child and a virtual classmate performed equally on a task, the teacher praised the child, the classmate, both, or neither. Contrary to hypotheses, there was no evidence that praise made children feel less smart, think that the teacher believed they were less smart, or experience elevated physiological arousal (heart rate, heart rate variability, blushing, skin conductance). Study 2 suggests that children instead viewed praise as a sign of being liked by the teacher. Our studies offer robust evidence that teacher praise may not make children feel less smart.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of cash-out availability on online betting behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Barnabas Szaszi; Wei Yue Hung; Peter Szecsi; Pál Kolumbán; Márton Kolozsvári; Miklos Bognar; Arife Yesilöz; Mark Griffiths; Zsolt Demetrovics
articles_hidden.abstract: The rise of online sports betting, facilitated by technological innovations such as the cash-out feature, has transformed the gambling landscape. While cash-outs have been suggested to intensify problematic gambling behaviors, empirical studies to date have been correlational, leaving a gap in determining causal evidence. In the present Registered Report, the proposed study will investigate the direct impact of the perceived availability of the cash-out feature on various facets of gambling behavior in an online experiment. Hungarian residents with online gambling history will be informed that they will have the chance to gamble with real money on sports events. Following random allocation, half of the participants will be told that they will have the option to cash out their bets before the outcome of the sports event is known, while the other half will not. The study will compare the proportion of participants placing bets, bet sizes, and bet risks between the two groups. Furthermore, the study will explore the differential effects of the cash-out feature on specific high-risk subgroups. The findings are likely to have significant implications for the design of online betting platforms, contribute to regulatory frameworks, and inform the design of interventions aimed at minimizing gambling-related harm.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical distinguishability of psychopathology symptom network and common factor models in longitudinal data
articles_hidden.authors: Sakari Johannes Lintula; Jaakko Tammilehto; Suoma Saarni; Tom Rosenström
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric conceptualizations of psychopathology have gained popularity. Most prominent approaches are the common factor (CF) and the symptom network models. A known problem in theory development through empirical findings is the statistical indistinguishability of CF and symptom network models in cross-sectional data. However, the extent of this problem and its implications have not been inspected formally for longitudinal studies. In this study, we sought to clarify the distinguishability between CF and symptom network models in longitudinal designs. We show necessary and sufficient conditions for indistinguishability in covariance for commonly applied vector autoregressive symptom network models and CF models and suggest a procedure for assessing whether a CF model can be refuted based on an estimated symptom network model. We give easy-to-implement R -functions for conducting the comparison. Numerical and empirical examples show that potential indistinguishability is relevant when interpreting the published literature. Overall, this study promotes comparative analysis of symptom network and CF models.

articles_hidden.title: Familiar words iconicity shapes novel words meaning
articles_hidden.authors: Daniele Gatti; Celia Martínez Tomás; José Antonio Hinojosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Iconicity, the perceived resemblance between a word’s form and meaning, is systematically related to the semantic organization of familiar vocabulary. This raises the possibility that iconicity-related regularities also constrain how people interpret unfamiliar words. We tested this proposal by learning mappings from (sub)lexical representations to large-scale English iconicity ratings and examining whether predicted iconicity for pseudowords was associated with the semantic quality and specificity of human-generated definitions. Higher iconicity predicted from semantic representations was associated with definitions that aligned more closely with their target pseudowords and distinguished them more selectively from alternative forms. In contrast, orthographic features predicted iconicity in familiar words but showed no corresponding associations with pseudoword definitions. The positive associations for semantic representations generalized across multiple encoders, including analyses in which different models were used to predict iconicity and evaluate definitions. These findings suggest that iconicity-related semantic structure in familiar vocabulary is associated with the construction of meanings for unfamiliar forms. They are consistent with discriminative and complementary learning accounts in which previously acquired form-meaning relations provide graded constraints on novel interpretations and, more broadly, they connect theories of iconicity grounded in perceptual and experiential resemblance with distributional accounts of lexical knowledge, suggesting that linguistic experience organizes and supports the generalization of resemblance-related semantic information to novel forms.

articles_hidden.title: Shared Cause Adjusted Mediation (SCAM): Introduction of method with empirical applications
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: A genuine mediated effect, also called an indirect effect, is the part of the relationship between a predictor (X) and an outcome (Y) that operates through a third variable, called a mediator (M). However, estimated mediated effects do not prove genuine mediation as they only require variables to be correlated and correlations may be due to confounding. Here, I propose adjusting for effects that are expected if the predictor, outcome, and mediator(s) share a common latent cause. In an application of this method on four studies using serial mediation analyses, only 5 of 24 (21%) reported effects remained statistically significant after such adjustment for a shared latent cause.

articles_hidden.title: Testing implications of the network theory of mental disorders in intensive short-term treatment
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Benz; Lea Schumacher; Samy Egli; Johannes Kopf-Beck
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance. Network theory is increasingly used to inform targeted and personalized treatment by identifying symptoms and interactions that maintain psychopathology. Yet, its prediction that successful treatment should weaken symptom interactions remains insufficiently tested.
Objective. To examine whether temporal interactions among depression and anxiety symptoms and global network connectivity decrease during short, intensive inpatient/day-clinic treatment, as predicted by network theory.
Design. Preregistered secondary analysis of OPTIMA, a randomized controlled trial conducted September 2017 to October 2020; analyses were conducted January 2025 to May 2026.
Setting. Single-center inpatient and day-clinic treatment in Germany with weekly symptom assessments.
Participants. Adults aged 18 to 75 years with moderate to severe depression without psychotic symptoms. Of 1370 patients assessed, 292 were randomized, and 288 were included in this analysis.
Interventions. Seven weeks of schema therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, or individual supportive therapy, with up to 2 individual and 2 group sessions weekly plus clinically indicated pharmacotherapy and concomitant care.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Changes in temporal interactions among 6 core depression and anxiety symptoms and in global network connectivity, estimated using a time-varying longitudinal network model. Exploratory stability landscapes characterized changes in network-implied symptom states.
Results. Among 288 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.6 [13.6] years; 55.6% female), only 3 of 36 temporal symptom associations changed substantially, although symptom severity decreased. Mean absolute network strength did not substantially decrease from 0.55 (95% CI, 0.47-0.64) at treatment start to 0.46 (95% CI, 0.38-0.54) after 7 weeks. Still, the network model could explain symptom trajectories well (Bayesian pseudo-R² ranging from 0.43 to 0.54) and exploratory network-implied stability landscapes indicated a system shift toward lower-symptom states.
Conclusions and Relevance. These findings provide limited support for the prediction that successful treatment reduces global connectivity in short, intensive treatment settings. In such settings, treatment-related change in symptom severity may be reflected in a reduction in general likelihood of symptom occurrence, but not necessarily in changes in symptom interactions, raising questions about long-term vulnerability. On the other hand, global symptom connectivity alone may not sufficiently characterize a healthy symptom system, and the role of specific symptom interactions warrants further investigation.
Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03287362.

articles_hidden.title: Inequality Can Increase Stealing, Reduce Trust, and Undermine Cooperation, Even When It Is Invisible
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Buzan; Daniel Nettle
articles_hidden.abstract: Higher inequality is associated with higher crime, lower trust, and lower cooperation, but the mechanisms producing these associations remain unclear. Inequality produces compositional effects through changing individuals’ resource levels, regardless of whether or not it is perceived. Inequality’s visibility may have further effects precisely because people perceive it. In Study 1 (N = 496; 64 groups), participants played a multiplayer experimental game in groups of eight, choosing to steal from one another, cooperate, or work alone. Participants’ were never informed of others' points levels. Inequality in the initial points distribution increased stealing rates, lowered trust, and reduced the rate of cooperation, but only when there was a points threshold below which it was disastrous to fall. Study 2 (N = 1,014; 132 groups) replicated these findings. It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others’ points, knew their partner’s points, or knew the group’s point distribution. Making inequality visible had no meaningful effect on any outcome. Together, these findings provide evidence for compositional, but not visibility, effects of inequality: distributing resources unequally around a threshold increased crime, reduced trust, and lowered cooperation, whether or not inequality was visible.

articles_hidden.title: Exploration for gains and loss-avoidance across the human lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Waltmann; Caroline Emily Phelps; Lorenz Deserno; Siyu Wang; Ben Eppinger; Robert C Wilson; Andrea M.F. Reiter
articles_hidden.abstract: Navigating an uncertain world, we constantly face the explore-exploit dilemma: should we stick with what we know, or explore options that may or may not prove better? An influential theory proposes that humans solve this dilemma through a division of labor in time: explore in childhood, exploit in old age. Our work adds critical empirical nuance to this theory. Exploration can manifest as deliberate information-seeking (“directed exploration”) or choice randomness (“random exploration”), and these strategies are employed differently for gain-seeking and loss-avoidance. Here, we ask how these modes of exploration relate to one another and jointly shape decision-making across the lifespan. A cross-sectional sample of 254 participants aged 8–79 performed a bandit task dissociating directed and random exploration in gain-seeking and loss-avoidance contexts. Factor analysis revealed three factors driving behavior: two domain-specific factors reflecting information-seeking for gains and loss-avoidance, respectively, and a domain-general factor reflecting choice randomness. Directed exploration for gains increased steadily and well into young adulthood before declining in older adulthood, whereas directed exploration for loss-avoidance changed little across the lifespan. Children and older adults, relative to young adults, were characterized by greater choice randomness across contexts, even when exploration was disadvantageous. Though working memory and processing speed accounted for some of these effects, independent effects of age remained. Our findings demonstrate that exploration is not a unitary phenomenon: it encompasses dissociable subprocesses – some domain-specific and others domain-general – with distinct developmental timelines that are shaped by cognitive maturation and decline as well as factors beyond cognitive ability.

articles_hidden.title: Perception of occluded motion depends on post-occlusion motion information
articles_hidden.authors: Lina Teichmann; Grace Edwards; Austin Kyle Behel; Chris Ian Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: Moving objects frequently become occluded from view, yet we often experience a compelling sense of their continued motion and position during occlusion. Despite this subjective impression, recent behavioral and neuroimaging evidence suggests that representations of moving objects during occlusion may be limited. In Experiment 1a, participants estimated the position of a moving object at unpredictable time points during occlusion. Position estimates were highly inaccurate, with errors increasing as objects travelled further behind the occluder. Increasing object speed exacerbated these errors in Experiment 1b, whereas decreasing speed improved performance. With decreased speed, there was also an increase in pre-occlusion motion information, which may aid object localization during dynamic occlusion. In Experiment 2, we found post-occlusion motion information could support accurate judgments of object reappearance. The necessity of post-occlusion information was further supported in Experiment 3, when removing post-occlusion motion information while testing a predictable intercept location resulted in inaccurate estimations. Across experiments, gaze position predicted behavioral errors, with eye movement strategies varying according to task demands. Together, these findings suggest that the position of moving objects is poorly represented during dynamic occlusion, despite our compelling subjective experience of their occluded location. Instead, accurate judgments depend critically on information acquired after the object re-emerges, consistent with a postdictive reconstruction of occluded object position.

articles_hidden.title: Chronic Pain as a Complex Dynamic System: Conceptual Foundations and a Narrative Review of Network Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Saskia Scholten; Gwen van der Wijk; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Felicitas Kininger; Julia Glombiewski; Johan W.S. Vlaeyen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Despite extensive medical, psychological, and social research and substantial healthcare investment, chronic pain remains highly prevalent, and a leading cause of years lived with disability. While multimodal and interdisciplinary treatments are recommended, progress may be limited by the lack of an integrative theoretical framework that captures the complexity of chronic pain across levels of analysis.
We introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework in which chronic pain emerges from interactions among biological, psychological, and social components over time, and we present a methodological toolbox based on the network approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling such interactions.
We conducted the first narrative review of network studies in chronic pain, identifying 54 studies published up to June 30, 2026. Most studies used cross-sectional network models to examine associations among pain-related variables, comorbidity patterns, and group differences, whereas longitudinal and within-person approaches were rare. Across studies, findings support the view that chronic pain-related factors form interconnected systems; however, substantial heterogeneity in variable selection and study design limits comparability and generalizability.
Overall, current applications provide an important first step toward modeling the complexity of chronic pain but so far remain limited in capturing temporal dynamics and individual-level processes. Advancing this field will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research that aligns network methods with system-level questions. In the longer term, this approach holds the promise to support the development of parsimonious models of key mechanisms, informing interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological Acceptance Across Adulthood: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lital Levit-Frank; Dikla Segel-Karpas; Nir Shalev
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological acceptance is an emotion regulation strategy in which people allow thoughts and feelings to arise and pass without trying to change them. Although theory implies that acceptance will increase with age, empirical evidence remains fragmented, with studies varying in sample characteristics, effect sizes, and age ranges. To address this gap and clarify the association between age and psychological acceptance we conducted a meta-analysis. Our preregistered search (PROSPERO CRD420251103979) identified 25 studies with 31 independent samples (N = 12,561). Random-effects pooling yielded a small but robust positive association between age and psychological acceptance (r = 0.077, 95% CI 0.027–0.127), despite substantial heterogeneity between studies. Specifically, studies that sampled wider age ranges reported stronger associations, so narrow age spans may understate the association.

articles_hidden.title: From Lab to App (and Back): A Conceptual Framework for Evidence-Based Digital Mental Health Interventions in Children and Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Solvejg Kassandra Kleber; Philipp Axel Raßbach; Hans-Henrik Dassow; Joschka Haltaufderheide; Elisabeth Höhne; Michael Kölch; André Markus; Nora Mierzwa; Robert Ranisch; Michael A Rapp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health problems represent a major global challenge, with access to appropriate care for children and adolescents remaining severely limited. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) can offer scalable, accessible support beyond traditional clinical settings. Despite a constantly growing number of youths DMHIs, the evidence base is constrained, due to a lack of replication and follow-up studies, scarce side-effect examination, and heterogeneous designs and characteristics. This is particularly concerning regarding young people as a vulnerable population. Knowledge of intervention processes is important to advance the field of DMHIs, while this topic is under researched in both DMHIs and traditional interventions for youth. Reaching full potential of DMHIs for youth requires an integrated research and development approach.

We consulted experts from multiple disciplines, including youths psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists, computer scientists and ethicists specializing in digital mental health, to integrate the current state of knowledge into a conceptual framework.

We outline that DMHIs are particularly well suited to generate insight into mechanisms of change and discuss key factors in DMHIs for youth. Furthermore, we address the need for more unified conceptualizations and standardized reporting and illustrate a working intervention process model for youths DMHIs to induce an overarching research agenda.
Overall, the framework provides a structured pathway toward scientifically rigorous and clinically meaningful digital innovation in youth mental health research and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Endogenous Attention Effects on Metacognitive Awareness: A Proof-of-Concept DLPFC-cTBS Study
