Objective: We investigated whether spatial attention modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency independently of perceptual sensitivity (d′), and whether the
DLPFC contributes to these effects.
Methods: Across two experiments, participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task embedded within a Posner cueing paradigm, utilizing adaptive
staircases. We assessed reaction times, signal detection metrics, subjective visibility ratings, and metacognitive efficiency. In Experiment 2, this task was performed following
continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) targeting either the bilateral DLPFC or an active control site (primary somatosensory cortex, S1).
Results: In Experiment 1, invalid cues prolonged reaction times, shifted response bias, and impaired metacognitive efficiency, without affecting overall accuracy, subjective
visibility, or perceptual sensitivity. In Experiment 2, whereas these attentional effects persisted following control S1-cTBS, they were significantly disrupted following DLPFC-cTBS, despite objective perceptual performance remaining stable. Furthermore, trial-by- trial analyses indicated that DLPFC disruption impairs adaptive metacognitive updating.
Conclusions: Endogenous spatial attention modulates visual metacognitive efficiency independently of objective perceptual sensitivity. Notably, our neuromodulatory findings suggest that the DLPFC does not generate metacognitive contents directly, but rather regulates the executive and attentional processes that inform metacognitive evaluations.

articles_hidden.title: Child and parent mental health symptoms in Nigeria: A genetically informed study of pre-school twins in a Low-/Middle-Income Country
articles_hidden.authors: Olakunle Oginni; Oluwatosin Olorunmoteni; Olusola Jeje; Olatokunbo Oguns; Kehinde Ayodele; Abimbola Onigbinde; Boladale Mapayi; Fruhling Rijsdijk; Anita Thapar; Frances Rice
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Ninety percent of the world’s children live in Low-/Middle-Income Countries (LMICs),
but relatively little is known about children’s mental health risk in these settings. Using a
genetically informative twin-family design, we estimated parent-child associations for mental
health symptoms (MHSs), indirect effects through specific risk/protective factors, and how
parental MHSs impact genetic/environmental influences on child MHSs in Nigeria.

Methods
We recruited 320 twin pairs (aged 3-5 years) and both parents in two Nigerian towns.
Participants were assessed for MHSs (emotional/behavioural symptoms in children; anxiety,
depressive and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder symptoms in parents), and selected
risk/protective factors (adverse home environments, adverse childhood experiences, poor
physical health; and religiosity, parental warmth and prosociality). We used structural equation
modelling to test parent-child MHS associations, and mediation by risk/protective factors. We
estimated latent genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and individual-specific environmental
(E) influences on child MHSs, and how parent MHSs impact these influences using univariate
twin models.

Results
Child MHSs were significantly associated with MHSs in both parents. The strongest
indirect effects for parent-child MHS associations were through adverse childhood experiences
and diminished parental warmth. Others indirect pathways involved poor physical health and
diminished prosociality. Latent A and C influences each explained 22-29% of the individual
differences in children’s MHSs. Independent of A influences, C influences were impacted by
parents’ MHSs.

Conclusion
Our findings indicate that potentially modifiable environmental pathways are important
for understanding parent-child MHS associations for very young children in a LMIC, and these
may inform intervention design. Larger and more rigorous genetically informative designs are
needed to replicate and extend our findings.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep and the Daytime Course of Anhedonia in Adolescent Depression: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah E. Marshall; Linda Nduka; Tahjanee Givens; Caroline M. Miller; Mollie Davis; Chana Engel; Kenneth Towbin; Daniel Pine; Katharina Kircanski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mounting evidence suggests that sleep disturbances and depression are linked through disruptions in reward processing. This pathway may be especially relevant to adolescent depression, as adolescence is characterized by more frequent sleep disturbances, reduced sleep, and refinement of reward circuitry.
Aim: This preregistered study uses high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression Studies (CTADS) cohort (collected from 2023 to 2026) to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia and to determine whether effects exhibit diurnal variation.
Methods: Sixty-five adolescents (12-18 years; 43 female, 22 male; 41 with major depressive disorder, 24 healthy volunteers) completed 120 EMA prompts over 30 days. Participants reported prior-night sleep disturbances and duration once per day, and anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia four times per day. We ran two Bayesian multilevel linear models, estimating anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, respectively, as functions of prior-night sleep disturbances, time of day, diagnostic group, and their interactions. We then ran two exploratory models assessing sleep duration in the same manner.
Results: In adolescents with MDD, whereas self-reported sleep disturbances did not predict anhedonia, longer sleep duration predicted both lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. In healthy adolescents, greater sleep disturbances predicted lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. Effects of sleep disturbances on anhedonia tended to increase across the day in adolescents with MDD and healthy adolescents.
Conclusions: Sleep disturbances and duration differentially predict next-day anhedonia in adolescents with MDD. For adolescent MDD patients, treatments that target sleep duration, as opposed to sleep disturbances, could provide more immediate effects on anhedonia. Time-of-day moderation effects suggest the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

articles_hidden.title: Data-informed online teacher training to improve student engagement during the transition to high school: a cluster randomised trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Noetel; Theresa Dicke; Philip David Parker; Nikos Ntoumanis; Mark R. Beauchamp; Alexander Yeung; Ryan Hulteen; Diego Vasconcellos; Asghar Ahmadi; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher-focused interventions typically select targets from a single motivational theory using researcher judgement. We tested whether data-informed target selection could improve student engagement during the transition to secondary school. Using elastic net regression on two-wave data from 1,799 students, we screened 71 teacher behaviours from four theories and identified the six (per subject) that best predicted engagement in physical education (PE) and mathematics. We randomised 20 low-socioeconomic-status schools to waitlist or a 12-hour, mostly online professional learning program targeting these behaviours, and recruited 10 high-socioeconomic-status comparison schools. In this pre-registered trial (1,877 Year 7 students; 27 schools analysed), the intervention did not improve engagement in any specification. No secondary outcome differed after multiple-comparison correction. Among students who completed baseline by the end of Week 1 of Year 7, the physical activity estimate favoured the intervention (d = 0.24) but did not survive correction and rested on only 4 intervention schools. Students did not report that intervention teachers used the targeted behaviours more. Data-informed target selection was feasible, but we found no evidence that this brief, mostly online program improved engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Differing Conceptions of Interpersonal and Intergroup Conflict Resolution Across the Lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Jacob Glassman; Katherine McAuliffe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conflicts between individuals and between groups are common across human relationships, making effective conflict resolution essential for flourishing societies. Yet, how conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflicts develop with age remains largely unexplored. We investigated perceptions of, expectations about, and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts in children (N = 97, Mage = 7.54, 45% female, 41% White), adolescents (N = 180, Mage = 13.17, 43% female, 59% White), and adults (N = 201, Mage = 38.98, 54% female, 78% White) tested in 2023. Participants viewed transgressions with ambiguous perpetrator intent between an individual perpetrator and an individual victim (interpersonal) or between a group perpetrator and a group victim (intergroup). All participants perceived more negative intent and expected less forgiveness in intergroup conflicts than in interpersonal conflicts, while adolescents and adults also punished more, and adults additionally expected less trust and perceived greater transgression severity. Harsher perceptions and expectations in intergroup relative to interpersonal conflicts were explained by greater intentionality being attributed to group perpetrators than individual perpetrators. With age, children increasingly perceived more negative intent and expected less trust in intergroup conflicts, appearing increasingly adultlike. Findings demonstrate that, compared with interpersonal conflicts, harsher conceptions of intergroup conflicts emerge early in development and strengthen across the lifespan.

Keywords: Conflict, conflict resolution, intergroup, interpersonal, social cognitive development

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Stoic Training on Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael William Lewis; Charles Kalarchian; Alexander MacLellan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Methods: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Results: Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = −2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = −0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = −0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = −0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions: Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

articles_hidden.title: The Third Allostasis: a biophysical displacement of regulatory purpose in neurodivergent, high-ability and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh)
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira; Pricilla Braga Laskosky
articles_hidden.abstract: Patients within the neurodivergent spectrum, high-ability profiles, and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh) frequently present a clinical paradox: marked cognitive domains alongside debilitating functional collapse, burnout, dysautonomia, and migrating multisystem symptoms. Standard cross-sectional laboratory investigations against population references routinely prove inconclusive or trigger fragmented, iatrogenic interventions. Here, we define the Third Allostasis: an evolutionarily conserved biophysical regime wherein the organism displaces peripheral homeostasis and lowers systemic throughput to defend central nervous system membrane viability when environmental and informational demands approach the kinetic limits of transmembrane ion clearance. Through within-person longitudinal follow-up of five adult HPCPh trajectories—spanning stepped recovery from decade-long containment, live entry into acute biological helplessness, endothelial–natriuretic decompression, cognitive restoration, and exit from chronic matrix dysautonomia—we demonstrate how this regime becomes clinically visible using four routine laboratory instruments. We introduce accessible arithmetic tools for any consulting room: the red-cell hydration index (Ht-3×Hb) and two "Rules of Three" (OsmP@290 and Na@290) that unmask hidden plasma osmolal gaps driven by uncharged organic osmolytes, even when raw osmolality and sodium remain within normal limits. Crucially, while an open osmolal gap signals fast-axis intercompartmental shift, clinical direction requires "whole-column reading" across slower coupled buffers, including circadian cortisol, tissue thyroid gating (FT3/rT3), iron-ferritin dynamics, prolactin, and monocytes. Recognizing the Third Allostasis shifts clinical practice from treating isolated organ abnormalities to reading the organism's adaptive effort as a whole, guiding contextual adjustments that relieve central overload and restore functional vitality.

articles_hidden.title: Current and Expected Well-Being in a Global Sample: The Role of Past Experiences, Current Circumstances, and Identity and Personality
articles_hidden.authors: Anaelle Gackiere; S. Mason Garrison; Christian Waugh
articles_hidden.abstract: People may use different processes to judge their current versus expected well-being. Using Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study (N = 98,412; 22 countries), we examined how predictors spanning past experiences, current circumstances, and identity and personality were associated with current and expected (five-year) well-being. We used stochastic search variable selection, a Bayesian method, to identify predictors reliably associated with each outcome, and focused interpretation on those with at least small effects. Participants generally expected their future well-being to exceed their current well-being. When each judgment was adjusted for the other, age and hope for the future showed opposite patterns: older participants reported lower, and more hopeful participants higher, expected well-being when controlling for current well-being. Much of the explained variance was shared across domains, and past experiences contributed little unique variance once current circumstances and identity and personality were accounted for; this suggests that the past may matter for well-being judgments largely through its links to people’s present lives. Our findings demonstrate that current and expected well-being draw on largely overlapping information that is weighted differently depending on whether people evaluate their current or expected lives.

articles_hidden.title: Talking in Timor-Leste: urbanization, peer input, and other influences on children's verbal environments
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph Coffey; Victoria Baranov; Xinran Hu; Diana Contreras Suarez; Lisa Cameron; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract: Children's early experiences with language are influenced by socioeconomic and cultural factors that vary greatly across societies. By expanding the geographical diversity of language acquisition studies, researchers are able to answer broader questions about mechanisms linking children’s speech input to their learning process. We present a large-scale study of 277 children between 11-58 months old growing up in Timor-Leste, an island nation in Southeast Asia. Children were drawn from households in 72 villages comprising both rural and urban communities. We used child-worn audio recorders combined with an open-source speaker diarization software to quantify their verbal input and production throughout the day. Our analysis found that children were exposed to 15 minutes of verbal input per hour total, mostly from other children and female adults. Of total input, 6 min/hour were produced during conversational exchanges with the child. Children from rural communities heard more adult vocalizations and vocalized more often than those sampled from urban communities. Older children and children with more siblings were exposed to more input from other children and vocalized more often themselves. Higher maternal education was associated with fewer child vocalizations. After adjusting for speaker misclassification, child vocalizations were significantly associated with input from other children and female adults. Our study indicates that verbal input from other children may be especially important in Timorese homes, and suggests that a positive relationship between education and adult input may not be universal. These results affirm the usefulness of long-form audio analysis for educators and policymakers interested in children’s early learning environments.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of perceptual salience and task load on executive vigilance: Independent and interacting effects without modulation of the vigilance decrement.
articles_hidden.authors: María Julieta Aguirre; Klara Hemmerich; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Pablo Barttfeld; Damián Baños Sáez; Juan Lupiáñez; Fernando Gabriel Luna
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To examine the independent and interacting effects of perceptual salience and task load on executive vigilance performance, as well as whether these factors modulate the vigilance decrement over time.
Background: Hits in vigilance tasks typically decline with time-on-task. This decrement is explained by the resource depletion of attentional resources (overload model) or to disengagement caused by task-unrelated thoughts (underload model). Previous research manipulated salience or task load separately, yielding inconsistent findings. Moreover, few studies have examined both factors simultaneously while holding other task parameters constant.
Method: Two preregistered studies and a pooled data analysis were conducted using the ANTI-Vea task, which assesses attention and vigilance components. In Study 1 (N = 84), perceptual salience of the target stimulus was manipulated between participants. In Study 2 (N = 45), perceptual salience and task load were orthogonally manipulated within participants. Study 3 reanalyzed combined data (N = 238) from Studies 1 and 2 together with data from previous research.
Results: Executive vigilance showed significant effects of perceptual salience and task load, with larger overall accuracy observed for the most salient targets and under moderate task load (dual-task condition). In signal detection measures, A′ was largest for the most salient targets, whereas moderate task load was associated with a less conservative response bias (B″). However, neither variable modulated the observed vigilance decrement over time.
Conclusion: Perceptual salience and task load affect overall executive vigilance but do not modulate its decrement over time-on-task. 
Application: Findings may inform the design of tasks and systems that optimize vigilance by promoting an optimal balance of task demands, by considering perceptual salience and task load to minimize failures and reduce the risk of vigilance decrement-related accidents.
Keywords: Vigilance, Executive vigilance, Perceptual salience, Task load, Vigilance decrement 
Précis: This study examined how perceptual salience and task load influence executive vigilance using the ANTI-Vea task. Across two preregistered studies and a pooled data analysis, overall performance varied across levels of task load and perceptual salience, but such manipulations did not modulate vigilance loss over time-on-task. Findings contribute to a fine-grained understanding of task-related factors that affect vigilance performance.

articles_hidden.title: Fixed Raters, Random Selection: A Correlation-Based Framework for Agreement ICCs in Two-Way Mixed-Effects Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Tzu-Yao Lin; francis tuerlinckx; Sophie Vanbelle
articles_hidden.abstract: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) quantify the reliability of measurements made on the same persons by different raters. In interrater reliability studies, consistency ICCs assess whether scores preserve the relative rankings of persons, while agreement ICCs evaluate the closeness of absolute scores across raters, thereby penalising systematic rater differences. In two-way mixed-effects designs, where raters are treated as fixed, conventional agreement ICCs raise a conceptual paradox: fixed-rater dispersion contributes to a source of disagreement despite the rater effects being constants, and it remains in the coefficient for all-rater averages even though those effects cancel in the average. In this paper, we resolve this paradox by introducing a finite-population sampling framework grounded in the correlation approach with hypothetical replications. Within this framework, we derive correlation-based agreement ICCs for both single ratings and all-rater averages, establishing a coherent probabilistic foundation that resolves the paradox. By considering various rater-sampling schemes, a family of agreement ICCs in mixed-effects designs is presented. We further show that the conventional agreement formulas can be recovered under independent sampling with replacement both within and between replicates. Thus, choosing an appropriate agreement ICC requires specifying how raters are sampled within and across replicates, rather than relying on the design alone.

articles_hidden.title: Ocular Phototherapy and Mental Health: What Vision Scientists and Clinicians Need to Know
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Bright light therapy is an effective and inexpensive non-pharmacological treatment for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) and, increasingly, for nonseasonal and bipolar depression. Its mechanism is a problem in vision science: light acts through the eye, chiefly through melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) working together with rods and cones. This narrative review, written for both vision scientists and clinicians, integrates research on ipRGC pathways to circadian, geniculate and mood-related brain regions; evidence from blind people with and without functioning ipRGCs; action spectra for melatonin suppression; trials comparing light spectra in SAD; ocular aging and safety; and clinical efficacy. Using published international standard tabulations, it also calculates melanopic dose, age-related loss and blue-light-hazard weighting for representative light sources. Narrow-band short-wavelength (blue-appearing) light outperforms dim long-wavelength (red-appearing) light in SAD but has not outperformed broadband white light, even though melatonin suppression peaks at 446–477 nm. Light rated at 10,000 photopic lux delivers between about 4,100 and 10,000 lux of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance, depending on its spectrum. The aging ocular media roughly halve the retinal melanopic dose between ages 25 and 75, although older adults may partly compensate physiologically, and compensating with added short-wavelength light increases blue-light-hazard-weighted exposure in the population with the highest prevalence of retinal disease. The therapeutic dose of light is therefore a retinal quantity that depends on spectrum, geometry, pupil size and age. The review closes with recommendations for prescribing and reporting light therapy and with open questions for both disciplines.

articles_hidden.title: Just-in-Time Neuromodulation: A Precision, State-Dependent Paradigm for On-Demand Brain Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Ashkan Rashedi; Aref Pariz; Jing Jin; Marzieh Zare; ANDRE RUSSOWSKY BRUNONI; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuromodulation is commonly delivered on fixed schedules, whereas psychiatric and neurological symptoms fluctuate over time. Just-in-Time Neuromodulation (JiT-NM) offers a framework for aligning intervention with the emergence or escalation of clinically relevant neural or symptomatic states. We propose three essential components: targeting the desired state, a state-detection system, and a neuromodulatory intervention capable of acting within a clinically useful time window. A fourth, optional component, adaptive personalization, may refine detection models and stimulation parameters over time. JiT-NM may support self-initiated or autonomous delivery, open-loop or closed-loop control, informed by automated symptom recognition or self-report, physiological signals, digital phenotyping, or wearable neural sensing. Established responsive and adaptive implanted stimulation systems provide clinical precedents, while early investigations in psychiatric disorders support further exploration. We discuss how neuroimaging-derived targets and biomarkers might be translated into compact, individualized sensing-and-stimulation systems, emphasizing the need to validate reliable state detection with fewer sensors. Key challenges include demonstrating the added value of intervention timing, accommodating changing neural dynamics, establishing real-world usability, as well as addressing safety, privacy, and regulatory requirements. JiT-NM provides a framework for investigating whether on-demand, state-based stimulation can complement scheduled treatment or achieve superior outcomes while reducing unnecessary treatment burden.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Treatment Preferences of Individuals Incarcerated at a Women’s Prison
articles_hidden.authors: Talia Rachel Cohen; Valerie Nguyen; Michael Koenigs
articles_hidden.abstract: The prevalence of mental illness is particularly high for incarcerated women.  Numerous conventional supports for mental wellbeing are unavailable due to incarceration-specific environmental factors (e.g., restrictions on movement, separation from support systems, dorm or segregation living). Thus, the same strategies used to treat mental illness in the community may not necessarily translate to carceral settings, and a clearer understanding of the unique experiences and preferences of incarcerated individuals is needed. The current project surveyed individuals at a women’s prison about their mental health treatment preferences. Results showed high favorability for mental health treatment across the board, with the highest ratings for self-administered treatment options. Participants also preferred Department of Corrections (DOC) providers to peer providers and individual support to group support. Clinical considerations for the DOC are discussed, including prioritizing confidentiality, investing in self-administered options, incorporating individualized elements into group programming, and using preference surveys to inform resource allocation.

articles_hidden.title: Binding Memory and Relational Mechanisms: The Central Role of Binding in Fluid Intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: William Frederick Garvey; Alon Zivony; Alicia Forsberg; Claudia Christina von Bastian
articles_hidden.abstract: Fluid intelligence (Gf) and working memory (WM) are strongly correlated, with the binding hypothesis suggesting that this relationship is driven by the capacity to bind content to context. However, it remains unclear how various binding functions overlap and relate to Gf. This study investigates the extent of overlap between five binding functions (item-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding) and their relationship with Gf. A sample of 174 young adults completed three visuospatial variants of tasks measuring these five binding functions alongside three Gf tasks. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and latent network analysis to evaluate shared and unique variances. Results indicated significant overlap among the binding functions, with item-to-location and item-to-item binding best modeled as a single latent variable termed binding memory. The shared variance among binding memory and the remaining binding functions was represented by a higher-order, process-general latent factor labeled Binding which was found to be statistically isomorphic with Gf. Latent network analysis further revealed that binding memory, relational integration, and relation processing each exhibited unique, direct relationships with Gf, whereas perceptual feature binding related to Gf only indirectly. These findings indicate that an overarching, domain-general ability to form and utilize bindings in a goal-directed manner is deeply intertwined with Gf, supporting theories emphasizing binding and relational mechanisms in Gf.

articles_hidden.title: The Precision Trap: On the Idealization of Mathematics in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Sepehrdad Rahimian
articles_hidden.abstract: Calls for greater precision and mathematization in psychology are often motivated by the hope that they will help overcome the field's theoretical problems. While mathematics undoubtedly contributes to scientific progress, this paper questions the idea that an increase in mathematization, in itself, constitutes progress. First, it examines the tradeoffs of precision, arguing that making a theory more precise can change what is being studied, reduce its functionality, and sometimes lend an unwarranted authority to its claims. It also considers examples of non-mathematical yet successful psychological approaches. Second, the paper introduces the Mathematization Bind. Under a realist standard, mathematical precision cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to Reality, as the history of the luminiferous aether illustrates. Under a pragmatic standard, the value of mathematics depends on what it enables us to accomplish, relative to the goals of inquiry. Neither perspective justifies treating greater mathematization as scientific progress by default. The paper also questions the tendency to regard an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific maturity. It concludes that the appropriate role and degree of mathematization in psychology should be determined by what it actually contributes to scientific inquiry, rather than by expectations about what a mature science ought to look like.

articles_hidden.title: When One Random Effect Is Not Enough: Mixture Model Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Caspar J. Van Lissa
articles_hidden.abstract: Handling between-study differences in effect sizes, or heterogeneity, is a key challenge in meta-analysis.  The common assumption that heterogeneity is normally distributed implies an absence of systematic sources of heterogeneity, or known and measured sources of heterogeneity that can be controlled using moderator analysis.  These assumptions fall short when effect sizes originate from multiple unknown subpopulations - for example, due to different research traditions, unmeasured moderators, publication bias, and outliers.  It has been argued that finite mixture models - also known as latent class analysis (LCA) - can capture these unobserved subgroups,  but there is currently no generalized framework for estimating such models.  We introduce open source software for estimating random-effects mixture, or "remix" meta-analyses.  Implemented in `OpenMx`, these structural equation models can be fully customized and further extended.  We conducted a simulation study to evaluate the `remix` algorithm's convergence, bias and confidence interval coverage,  and the performance of several class enumeration metrics: the AIC, BIC, and ICL information criteria, predictive model comparison (PMC), and cross-validation.  Results show that the method is fast and has low bias, but confidence interval coverage is below nominal levels,  and class enumeration remains challenging - which are known limitations of LCA.  Nevertheless, remix meta-analysis is the appropriate method when effect sizes originate from a mixture of unobserved subpopulations; a scenario which is arguably commonplace in meta-analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Altered Temporality: Human-Validated LLM Analysis of Naturalistic Trip Reports
articles_hidden.authors: Paweł Gładziejewski; Aleksander Milczanowski; Bogna Bylicka; Jan Nikadon
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychedelic substances can profoundly alter the experience of time, yet we lack a detailed account of which distinct temporal alterations occur, how prevalent they are, and how they are interrelated. A key obstacle is that the methods best suited to capturing the phenomenological repertoire of altered temporality are difficult to scale and may therefore fail to reliably capture rare phenomena, whereas scalable psychometric tools lack the categorical resolution to tease apart distinct types of experience. Here we combine resolution with scale, applying a theorist-constructed phenomenological codebook to naturalistic psychedelic trip reports through large language model (LLM)-based, corpus-scale content analysis. First, we establish that altered temporality resolves into seven textually distinguishable categories, recovered with similar reliability by human and LLM coders. Second, we apply LLM-based qualitative analysis to 3,291 excerpts from a corpus of 7,303 psychedelic trip reports, confirming that this categorical structure holds at corpus scale. Third, we estimate category prevalence and identify a stable associative structure comprising a complex of rare, interconnected alterations centered on timelessness and metaphysical appraisals, alongside an independent, more prevalent alteration in the subjective rate and duration of temporal flow. Fourth, we show that a similar relative prevalence profile and broad associative pattern, derived from the English-language Shroomery corpus, replicate in the independent Polish-language Neurogroove repository. Our study provides a high-resolution map of psychedelic temporality, arrived at by a method that may generalize beyond it, toward recovering the taxonomic structure of altered states of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal Associations Between Cannabis Initiation and  Recurrent Binge Eating Onset in US Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Kavish Chapra; Ya-Wen Chang; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Cannabis use and binge eating often co-occur; however, the order and timing of their onset are not well described in population-based samples, limiting our understanding of potential risk pathways between the two behaviors. 

Method: We examined the order and timing of onset of these behaviors among 12,314 adults from the Collaborative Psychiatric Epidemiology Surveys. Cannabis initiation and recurrent binge eating (i.e., binge eating at least twice weekly for 3 months) were dated using ages of onset reported at a single interview. Survey-weighted survival and discrete-time models estimated cumulative probabilities and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for onset of each behavior after the other. 

Results: Among 251 adults reporting both behaviors, cannabis initiation came first for 62.3% (95% CI [52.9, 71.7]) and binge eating came first for 33.2% (95% CI [23.8, 42.5]). The median interval between behaviors was 4 to 5 years. Within 10 years of cannabis initiation, 2.6% (95% CI [1.7, 3.6]) had reported binge eating onset; in contrast, within 10 years of binge eating onset, 35.6% (95% CI [24.7, 45.0]) had reported cannabis initiation. Prior cannabis initiation was associated with higher annual odds of binge eating onset (OR = 2.23, 95% CI [1.46, 3.39], p < .001), and prior binge eating was associated with higher annual odds of cannabis initiation (OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.07, 2.42], p = .024). In secondary analyses, the association of prior cannabis initiation with binge eating onset was significant among women (OR = 2.63, p < .001) but not men (OR = 1.81, p = .113). The sex interaction was not significant after correction (q = .063). 

Conclusions: Each behavior was associated with later onset of the other, suggesting a two-way association rather than a single direction of influence. Thus, clinicians treating either behavior should consider asking about the other. However, because onset ages were recalled, prospective research is critical to test causal direction.

articles_hidden.title: The Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker: Mental Sampling Processes Capture Preference, Confidence and Response Time in Risky Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Spicer; Yun-Xiao Li; Lucas Castillo; Johanna Falben; Stella Qian; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract: Modern models of preferential decision making have achieved substantial success in predicting choice behaviour both qualitatively and quantitatively, but often overlook related aspects such as response time or confidence. In parallel, recently proposed mental sampling frameworks have offered broad explanations for multiple aspects of behaviour including probability judgments, perceptual estimates and numerical forecasts, but have not yet been applied to preferential choice. Here, we seek to unite these lines of research by extending one such framework, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS; Zhu et al., 2024), to decisions between alternatives which differ in the value of their potential outcomes. We present a new version of the ABS adapted to such decisions, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker (ABDM), able to predict not just choices, but also reaction times and confidence in selections. We compare the predictions of the ABDM against extant choice and response time data in risky choice tasks, finding strong correspondence in both. We also contrast the new model against leading explanations for behaviour in such tasks, showing the ABDM is competitive in choice and ahead in response times. We thus propose this model as a broader approach to decision making capable of explaining multiple measures from a common process.

articles_hidden.title: What Is a “Blank” Mind? Testing the Meaning and Construct Validity of Mind-Blanking Reports to Thought Probes
articles_hidden.authors: Chandni Lal; Matt Welhaf; Michael J. Kane
articles_hidden.abstract: Four studies evaluated probed mind-blanking reports, an off-task conscious state ostensibly experienced as an absence of thought and subjective experience. We examined whether people make mind-blanking reports to indicate uncertainty about their preceding thoughts, rather than to communicate an experienced “blank;” we also assessed whether subjects used “blank” to refer to the absence of experience, or rather an unclear, diffuse form of experience. U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include “I-don’t-know” and “mind-blanking” options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463–790). Within an online go/no-go task, we tested whether different response options yielded different rates of mind-blanking and I-don’t-know reports. That is, would mind-blanking rates be higher when an “I don’t know” response option was not available, suggesting that mind-blanking reports indicate uncertainty? Would rates of I-don’t-know reports be lower when the “mind-blanking” option was unavailable? Neither mind-blanking nor I-don’t-know report rates differed significantly between probe-type conditions. Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories. Subjects didn’t use mind-blanking reports to reflect uncertainty. Study 3 (N = 415) extended our construct-validity investigation to the phenomenology of mind-blanking by separating (within subjects) “mind-blanking” response options into “unclear or foggy thoughts” versus “complete absence of experience.” Unclear thoughts accounted for 3% of thought reports, versus 1% reflecting no experience, suggesting that “blanking” more often reflects diffuse than absent subjective states.

articles_hidden.title: Chronic Pain as a Complex Dynamic System: Conceptual Foundations and a Narrative Review of Network Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Saskia Scholten; Gwen van der Wijk; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Felicitas Kininger; Julia Glombiewski; Johan W.S. Vlaeyen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Despite extensive medical, psychological, and social research and substantial healthcare investment, chronic pain remains highly prevalent, and a leading cause of years lived with disability. While multimodal and interdisciplinary treatments are recommended, progress may be limited by the lack of an integrative theoretical framework that captures the complexity of chronic pain across levels of analysis.
We introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework in which chronic pain emerges from interactions among biological, psychological, and social components over time, and we present a methodological toolbox based on the network approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling such interactions.
We conducted the first narrative review of network studies in chronic pain, identifying 54 studies published up to June 30, 2026. Most studies used cross-sectional network models to examine associations among pain-related variables, comorbidity patterns, and group differences, whereas longitudinal and within-person approaches were rare. Across studies, findings support the view that chronic pain-related factors form interconnected systems; however, substantial heterogeneity in variable selection and study design limits comparability and generalizability.
Overall, current applications provide an important first step toward modeling the complexity of chronic pain but so far remain limited in capturing temporal dynamics and individual-level processes. Advancing this field will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research that aligns network methods with system-level questions. In the longer term, this approach holds the promise to support the development of parsimonious models of key mechanisms, informing interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Replication Research
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin McManus
articles_hidden.abstract: Replication studies are essential for building cumulative knowledge in second language acquisition (SLA) research because they allow researchers to revisit, contextualize, and extend the findings of earlier studies. Rather than arguing for the value of replication, this chapter focuses on the replication research process itself. It begins with two core issues: deciding what study to replicate and what kind of replication to conduct (conceptual, approximate, close, or exact). It then considers the place of replication in qualitative research. The chapter reviews methodological considerations for planning a replication, supported by a set of planning questions, and for disseminating it through presentations and journal articles, including reporting standards. It then describes the practical relevance of replication for building confidence in findings before they are applied and for testing lab-based results in classrooms. The chapter closes with future directions: integrating replication into research programs, extending it beyond quantitative methods, improving planning and reporting, and adopting open research practices.

articles_hidden.title: A Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial of a Transdiagnostic Preventative Mental Health Intervention for Adolescents: Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training (ReSET)
articles_hidden.authors: Pasco Fearon; Alex Lloyd; Peter Martin; Roslyn Law; Laura Lucas; Tom Chin-Han Wu; Nick Midgley; Nikolaus Steinbeis; René Veenstra; Jaime Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: Rates of mental health problems in adolescents have increased in the last decade, prompting urgent calls for effective, scalable preventative interventions. To determine whether a novel, group-based, transdiagnostic indicated prevention programme (Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training; ReSET), delivered through existing school mental health provision, improves mental health and wellbeing in at-risk adolescents.
Methods: Two-arm cluster randomised controlled superiority trial (1:1) evaluating ReSET plus usual care versus usual care only, with outcomes assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up. Adolescents aged 12–14 identified through whole-school screening as scoring in the top 25th percentile for overall psychopathology symptoms, in schools selected to over-represent high-need communities (≥30% free school meals eligibility). ReSET is an 8-session group -based intervention that targets two key mechanisms implicated in risk for psychopathology in adolescents – social functioning and emotional processing. Pre-registered co-primary outcomes were overall self-reported psychopathology (SDQ) and wellbeing (WEMWBS), assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up.
Results: Of 4,005 adolescents screened, 1465 met eligibility, 727 consented and 560 were enrolled. There was no evidence of intervention effects on either co-primary outcome immediately post-intervention. At 12-month follow-up, there was evidence of improvement in overall psychopathology (adjusted mean difference −1.36, 97.5% CI −2.23 to −0.50, p=0.0004; SMD=0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.42). Secondary outcomes showed a consistent pattern: no effects immediately post-intervention, but significant benefits for anxiety, depression, general psychopathology, and internalising symptoms at 12-month follow-up. No effects on externalising symptoms were observed at either timepoint.
Conclusions: The delayed emergence of benefit is consistent with a skills-based prevention model in which adolescents acquire skills that support resilient functioning when facing subsequent emotional and interpersonal challenges. These findings suggest that transdiagnostic interventions targeting socioemotional processes have the potential to prevent common adolescent mental health problems, though replication and longer-term evaluation are needed.

articles_hidden.title: The plurality of metacognition: Historical origins and research traditions
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Sebastián Barrientos
articles_hidden.abstract: Metacognition is commonly defined as the monitoring and control of one’s own cognition, yet the term covers related phenomena that differ in their theoretical organisation, assessment, and application. This historically oriented narrative review examines how the convergence of cognitive, developmental, and educational research traditions produced this plurality. It reconstructs the construct’s empirical and theoretical antecedents in memory monitoring, children’s knowledge of cognition, and strategic regulation of learning, and compares influential accounts in terms of their explanatory aims, central components, and levels of analysis. The comparison shows that different traditions came to emphasise metacognitive knowledge, experiences, monitoring, regulatory activity, or the functional relation between object- and meta-level cognition. These differences are interpreted not as competing definitions of an identical phenomenon, but as reflecting the distinct problems and methods from which each account developed. The review argues that metacognition is best approached as a historically assembled family of related but partially non-interchangeable facets, without assuming either complete unity or fragmentation. This interpretation clarifies why indicators derived from different traditions often diverge, and why specifying the facet, function, and level of analysis intended by the term should be a condition for cumulative research across theory, measurement, and application.

articles_hidden.title: Root Causes and Prevention of Mobility Device Damage During Air Travel: A Rapid Review
articles_hidden.authors: Zeyad Ghulam; Alison Whiting; Tilak Dutta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The primary objective of this rapid review is to identify peer-reviewed academic literature that discusses the root causes of mobility device damage and loss during air travel, and to synthesize the operational strategies for preventing this damage.
Introduction: Air travel provides essential access to education, healthcare, employment, and leisure. However, persons with disabilities remain vastly underrepresented among air travelers and overrepresented in aviation complaint statistics. A failure point in the accessible travel chain is the damage, loss, or delayed return of mobility devices. While general accessibility reviews categorize device damage as a physical barrier, few investigate the specific cargo-handling mechanisms, securement failures, and design limitations that cause these incidents.

Inclusion Criteria: This review will include peer-reviewed literature focusing on travelers who use mobility devices. The primary concept is the damage, loss, or delayed return of these devices, alongside proposed preventive strategies or root-cause analyses. The context is restricted to commercial air travel operations, including ground handling, cargo stowage, and terminal transfers.

Methods: This protocol strictly adheres to the Cochrane Rapid Review Methods Group recommendations. Searches will be executed in Medline, Scopus and Web of Science (Core Collection). Title and abstract screening, full-text reviews and data extraction will be managed in Nested Knowledge. To expedite the process, a primary reviewer will conduct screening and data extraction, with a secondary reviewer independently piloting tools, screening all excluded records, and verifying data and risk-of-bias assessments. Evidence will be synthesized narratively, prioritizing high-quality study designs to inform operational mitigation.

articles_hidden.title: Inter-trial intervals bias reinforcement learning in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Noa Yadid; Omer Linkovski; Paul B. Sharp
articles_hidden.abstract: Although we know humans attempt to maximize reward per unit time when foraging, it remains unclear how the common practice of varying waiting time via inter-trial intervals (ITI) impacts reinforcement learning. Here, we tested several hypotheses concerning how time to wait during the ITI impacts reinforcement learning, including replay of recent outcomes, sensory decay of action representations, and discounting of action values due to added time costs. To test which of these accounts explains how ITIs impact reinforcement learning, we conducted a series of bandit-style tasks in which the ITI was either 1 or 4 seconds, expecting longer ITIs to allow replay that strengthens recent learning. Instead, across four studies (n = 96, 96, 439 and 117), a longer ITI made people more likely to change their last choice selectively after wins but not after losses. To explain why this effect occurs, we used computational modeling to demonstrate how the ITI cost competes with learned value for control of the next choice, with time costs impacting choice more when learned values were more uncertain. The effect of ITIs on choice generalized to a public fMRI dataset with jittered ITIs, and was absent in language-model agents playing our task. Taken together, our results suggest that ITIs bias human reinforcement learning, where people try to reduce uncontrollable time costs through switching to a new choice.

articles_hidden.title: Experiment-based calibration in psychology: foundational and data-generating model
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik R Bach
articles_hidden.abstract:
Experiment-based calibration is a novel method for measurement validation, which – unlike classical validity metrics – does not require stable between-person variance. In this approach, the latent variable to be measured
is manipulated by an experiment, and its predicted scores – termed standard scores – are compared against the measured scores. Previous work has shown that under plausible boundary conditions, the correlation
between standard and measured scores – termed retrodictive validity – is informative about measurement accuracy, i.e. combined trueness and precision. Here, I expand these findings in several directions. First, I
formalise the approach in a probability-theoretic framework with the concept of a standardised calibration space. Second, I relate this framework to classical validity theory and show that the boundary conditions
in fact apply to any form of criterion validity, including classical convergent validity. Thus, I state precise and empirically quantifiable boundary conditions under which criterion validity metrics are informative on
validity. Third, I relate these boundary conditions to confounding variables, i.e. correlated latent variables. I show that in the limit, calibration will converge on the latent variable that is most closely related to the
standard. Finally, I provide a framework for modelling the data-generating process with Markov kernels, and identify sufficient conditions under which the data generation model results in a calibration space. In sum,
this article provides a formal probability-theoretic framework for experiment-based calibration and facilitates modelling and empirical assessment of the data generating processes.

articles_hidden.title: Virtual Reality Simulation of Prosthesis embodiment: A Multimodal Investigation Examining Gaze Behaviour and Sense of agency
articles_hidden.authors: David Crevillén Hernández; Bigna Lenggenhager; Cosimo Gentile; Laura Zapparoli; Roberto Meattini; Gianluca Saetta; Emily S. Cross
articles_hidden.abstract: Suffering a limb amputation has a major impact on physical and psychological health, with prosthetic devices being a fundamental tool to mitigate it. Prosthesis embodiment (integrating a prosthetic device into the bodily self) is a fundamental process for accepting these devices, with the sense of agency (the experience of controlling one’s actions and, through them, the course of external events) as a key contributing factor. Current upper-limb myoelectric prostheses still present high abandonment rates, partly due to motor-control errors that may reduce the sense of agency associated with prosthesis movements. One possible solution is sharing motor autonomy between the user and a grasping intention-detection algorithm, with prosthetic movements combining user actions and inferred intentions. In this study, we investigated whether shared autonomy, simulated through automated grasp assistance by an idealised intention-detection system in immersive virtual reality, influences explicit (self-reported) and implicit (indirectly assessed) sense of agency, prosthesis embodiment, task performance, and gaze behaviour. Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance. Shared autonomy increased self-reported agency and reduced failed attempts. However, neither appearance nor motor autonomy affected embodiment scores. Although explicit and implicit measures of agency were significantly correlated, they responded differently to experimental manipulations. Shared autonomy increased explicit but not implicit agency, while longer action–outcome delays were associated with reduced explicit agency but stronger intentional binding.  revealing dissociations across conditions and action-outcome delays. Additionally, explicit agency was associated with reduced visual attention towards the prosthesis and manipulated object. Together, these results indicate that shared autonomy approaches can enhance control experience and improve task performance while highlighting distinctions between explicit and implicit agency measures during prosthesis control.

articles_hidden.title: When Effort Invigorates:  Instrumental Effort History Increases Cue-Evoked Response Vigour While Preserving Outcome-Specific Transfer
articles_hidden.authors: Yulong Huang; Zhang Chen; Ruth Krebs; Lara Bardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental cues can influence action through outcome-related information learned elsewhere, but whether features of the instrumental acquisition history associated with those outcomes remain behaviourally relevant when the outcomes are later predicted by Pavlovian cues is unknown. Across two experiments, one conducted in the laboratory (N = 54) and one online (N = 67), we separated instrumental acquisition under low- and high-effort response requirements from Pavlovian cue learning. Participants first learned that different actions produced outcomes under relatively low or high effort requirements and separately learned cues predicting those same outcomes. Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) was then tested under extinction, with neither outcomes nor response requirements present. In both experiments, reward-predictive cues elicited greater response vigour than a control cue. Critically, cues predicting outcomes previously obtained under high-effort response requirements elicited greater responding than cues predicting outcomes obtained under low-effort requirements. Specific PIT was robust under both acquisition conditions, with cues selectively promoting actions associated with their predicted outcomes. There was also suggestive evidence that high-effort acquisition amplified the magnitude of specific PIT, but this modulation was not consistently supported across experiments or statistical approaches. No corresponding effect emerged for initial outcome-congruent action selection. Overall, response vigour was modulated by instrumental effort history more consistently than outcome-specific action selection, indicating that features of prior effortful instrumental experience can remain behaviourally relevant when the associated outcomes are later predicted by separately learned Pavlovian cues.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between deictic relating and theory of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Maura Nevejans; Jamie Cummins; Jan De Houwer; Emiel Cracco; Yulong Huang; Jan R. Wiersema
articles_hidden.abstract: Relational Frame Theory (RFT) proposes that deictic relating plays a critical role in “Theory of Mind” (ToM). However, empirical research to date on the relationship between deictic relating and ToM has been inconclusive, potentially due to small sample sizes and limitations in the assessment of deictic relating. In the present online study (N = 164), we tested the relationship between deictic relating and two ToM measures: a low-level ToM task (a visual perspective-taking task) and a high-level ToM task (the Faux Pas Recognition Test). We additionally tested associations with general cognitive ability and autism traits. Based on predictions from RFT, we hypothesized that deictic relating would correlate with both ToM measures, with a stronger association for low-level ToM. We observed a positive correlation of deictic relating with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, whereas its correlation with visual perspective-taking was non-significant for our primary outcome measure. Opposite to predictions derived from RFT, deictic relating was positively correlated with autism traits, whereas scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test and visual perspective-taking task were not significantly correlated with autism traits. Although these findings may suggest a relationship between deictic relating and ToM, the absence of an association with low-level ToM is difficult to reconcile with RFT. Alternative explanations for observed correlations, including task characteristics or other related abilities, are discussed. Finally, the finding that higher scores on the autism traits questionnaire were related to better deictic relating is at odds with RFT and raises questions about which abilities the task measures.
